Madam Speaker, I rise under the provisions of Standing Order 43 on the most tragic and important issue facing Canada at this moment, about which something could be done. Negotiations broke down completely in the Port of Vancouver work stoppage on Sunday afternoon. The Government should have moved immediately, on Monday morning, with negotiations broken off. It did not, and it has not moved till this time.
This work stoppage is costing Canada thousands of dollars while I stand here talking. This work stoppage means a loss to Canada of $1 million or more an hour; $8 million is being lost in wheat sales every day and more millions in other bulk shipments, as well as the human tragedies of lost work. As of 5.30 this morning, 86 ships were waiting in Vancouver-

speechtext:
Madam Speaker, the work stoppage at the major ports on the West Coast has, to date, cost grain producers over $100 million in lost sales. Sales are not being deferred, they are being lost. Our reputation as a reliable grain supplier to international markets is once again in jeopardy. To date the work stoppage has caused over 6,000 Canadians to be out of work.
Since 1972 Parliament has had to intervene in related grain handling and transportation disputes because it was recognized that labour and management difficulties simply do not justify the damage inflicted on the total economy. I move, under the provision of Standing Order 43, seconded by the Hon. Member for Swift Current-Maple Creek (Mr. Hamilton):
That this House consider designating the grain handling and transportation sectors as they affect grain exports, as essential services.

subsubtopic: HIGH COST OF FOOD AND DRY GOODS
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, 1 rise under the provisions of Standing Order 43 on a matter of the most urgent and pressing necessity. A recent survey conducted by my office revealed that basic food prices in northern communities were, on average, 80 per cent higher than those in Ottawa. Another survey, just completed, shows that dry goods prices in the Hudson's Bay store in Frobisher Bay are, on average, 28 per cent higher than those same goods in the Bay's Ottawa store, despite a commitment made two years ago by Bay officials that the differential would not exceed 10 per cent. I therefore move, seconded by the Hon. Member for Hamilton Mountain (Mr. Deans):
That the House call upon the Government to initiate a task force immediately to investigate all aspects of the cost of living crisis in the Far North.

speechtext: I have the honour to draw the attention of the House to the distinguished presence in our gallery of Legislative Assembly Presidents and Speakers, namely Mr. James Walding of Manitoba, Deputy Speaker Moore from New Brunswick, Speaker Russell from Newfoundland, President Vaillancourt from Quebec, Speaker Donahoe from Nova Scotia, and Deputy Speaker Muller from Saskatchewan-

speakeroldname: Right Hon. Joe Clark (Leader of the Opposition):
subsubtopic: WORK STOPPAGE AT WEST COAST PORTS-GOVERNMENT POSITION
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, my question is for the Prime Minister. It relates to the ports dispute on the West Coast. The Prime Minister will recall that he said in the House:
-That if the parties had not settled their dispute through the process of free collective bargaining by Monday night this Government would ensure in some way that the strike would be ended-
That repeated an undertaking given six days ago by the Minister of Finance. Can the Prime Minister tell us when the Government will be acting to open the ports, and what form that action will take?

speakeroldname: Right Hon. P. E. Trudeau (Prime Minister):
subsubtopic: WORK STOPPAGE AT WEST COAST PORTS-GOVERNMENT POSITION
speechtext:
Yes, I would be happy to answer the question asked by the Right Hon.

November 2, 1982
Oral Questions
Leader of the Opposition, Madam Speaker. We are sorry the process of free collective bargaining has not brought this regretful strike to an end. Today the House Leader will be giving notice of legislation-

subsubtopic: WORK STOPPAGE AT WEST COAST PORTS-GOVERNMENT POSITION
speechtext: It's a lockout.

subsubtopic: WORK STOPPAGE AT WEST COAST PORTS-GOVERNMENT POSITION
speechtext:
I beg your pardon, it is a lockout and it is a regrettable one. My point remains that we are sorry the parties have not been able to find a ground on which they could accommodate each other's points of view. Therefore, we will be giving notice today. We hope to be able to get the consent of the House to proceed with the legislation tomorrow. It would be the hope of this Government that there will be cooperation from all Parties to pass the legislation as soon as possible, hopefully dealing with all three stages within a day.
As a first stage the lockout would be ended and work could resume in the ports on the West Coast. Failing that, if the legislation has to be proceeded with, then the Government would intend applying the spirit of the six and five legislation.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. Joe Clark (Leader of the Opposition):
speechtext: Madam Speaker, the Prime Minister would know that this dispute is costing Canada at least $8 million a day. He is talking about introducing something today for action tomorrow. We on this side of the House would be prepared to deal today with legislation brought in today, and to deal with it in all stages.
Hear, hear!

In that light, will the Prime Minister agree to bring in that legislation today to seek agreement, which I hereby give on behalf of my party, to have it proceeded with today so that we will not waste $8 million and another day? Can we act today?

speakeroldname: Right Hon. P. E. Trudeau (Prime Minister):
speechtext: Madam Speaker, I am happy with the spirit of co-operation extended to Parliament by the Leader of the Opposition. I would expect that he would want Members of his own Party and Members of the New Democratic Party at least to know what the content of the legislation is before agreeing to pass it through all stages today.
Oh, oh!

That is why I thought it preferable to give a general indication of the content of the legislation which, once again, would entail an immediate return to work and an application of the six and five type of guidelines that were in the June budget, for this particular bargaining group. It is still our hope, in the knowledge that this is the intention of the Government and now of the Official Opposition, to introduce and pass this legislation in all stages, perhaps tomorrow, but I would still hope that this further delay, with the notice of the legislation and its general content, would permit both parties
to return to the bargaining table and to reach an agreement by the process of collective bargaining.

The Prime Minister speaks of what would be preferable. What would be preferable is to act today to resolve the dispute today and stop another $8 million, at least, of loss to the Canadian economy. That is what would be preferable today.
Hear, hear!

speakeroldname: Right Hon. Joe Clark (Leader of the Opposition):
speechtext: Will the Prime Minister tell the House whether this legislation of which he speaks is ready now, at 20 minutes after two o'clock, to be introduced in the House of Commons? Will he tell the House of Commons whether there are any negotiations proceeding between the Government and any political party in the House respecting the nature of that legislation?

speakeroldname: Right Hon. P. E. Trudeau (Prime Minister):
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I know of no negotiations proceeding at this time but I would hope that the announcement that I made in answer to a question from the Leader of the Opposition would incite the parties to return to the bargaining table and to reach an agreement through the process of free collective bargaining.
This Government would rather not legislate. We would want to see the strike end as soon as tomorrow, once again-
Lockout.

The lockout end as soon as tomorrow. It will if we have co-operation from all sides. We are still hopeful, and we find it preferable not-as the Leader of the Opposition suggests-to slam on a piece of legislation that he has not seen, his Party has not seen, that the New Democratic Party has not seen, and that the parties to the dispute have not seen.
I repeat to the Leader of the Opposition that to impose six and five on the bargaining parties is something that we would rather not do, but they are under notice now that we will do it with the obvious enthusiastic support of the Conservative Party if they cannot reach an agreement within a very short period of time.
Hear, hear!

speakeroldname: Right Hon. Joe Clark (Leader of the Opposition):
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I do not understand why the Government is stalling. The Minister of Finance gave a clear commitment that there would be action by Monday. The Prime Minister gave a clear commitment there would be action by Monday. Monday has passed. It is now Tuesday. Nothing has been done. The Prime Minister has indicated that he intends to do nothing today. Will the Prime Minister answer the question that I put earlier?
November 2, 1982

Is the legislation ready to be presented to Parliament today? Is it ready now?

speakeroldname: Right Hon. P. E. Trudeau (Prime Minister):
speechtext: Yes, Madam Speaker, the legislation is ready. I would be happy to know right now from the Leader of the Oppposition if he is prepared to debate this legislation unconditionally, sight unseen. If he is, we will be ready to proceed.
Hear, hear!

subtopic: MOVEMENT THROUGH CHURCHILL-UPGRADING OF RAILWAY FACILITIES
MOVEMENT THROUGH CHURCHILL-UPGRADING OF RAILWAY FACILITIES
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, in the absence of the Minister of Transport I will address my question to the Prime Minister. I am sure that the grain producers in western Canada are disappointed at the answers he has given to the Leader of the Opposition. The Prime Minister is well aware of the disastrous effect that the tie-up of the west coast ports is having on western agriculture. With low grain prices and losses in sales in the neighbourhood of $8 million a day, as well as the effect the port closure has on our credibility as an exporter, the time has come to examine the expansion of port facilities at Churchill in order to increase our export capacity and to act as a buffer in the event of strikes.
Can the Prime Minister advise the House whether or not the Minister of Transport has discussed the question of upgrading the facilities at Churchill with Canadian National Railways with a view to upgrading the line to handle hopper cars to carry grain and other commodities from western Canada?

I am wondering if the Prime Minister would consider setting up a task force comprised of Members of the Senate and the House of Commons to consider what can be done to ensure that farmers in western Canada will have recourse in order to make up the losses that they suffer from these disastrous strikes.

speakerposition: Minister responsible for the Status of Women; Minister of State (Mines)
subsubtopic: IRON ORE COMPANY CLOSING IN SCHEFFERVILLE, P.Q.
speechtext: Madam Speaker, this morning I held long discussions with the Iron Ore Company concerning the plight of the workers in Schefferville. I am happy to report that of the 285 workers who will be directly affected, at least 72 of whom will be taking pensions or early retirement, and perhaps more. The remaining workers will be receiving a very generous settlement, including two weeks' pay for every year of service, full vacation and extended vacation. They will be invited to stay on in their homes for the remainder of the winter and every effort will be made to help. We are co-ordinating a committee with the Department of Employment and Immigration to relocate these workers with full maximum use of government grants.

speakerposition: Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development
speechtext: Madam Speaker, if I may answer the Leader of the New Democratic Party with regard to Cyprus Anvil, let me just tell him that so far there has been a tripartite approach in an attempt to re-open the operation by this spring, at the latest.
A four-way approach.

speakerposition: Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development
speechtext:
It involves the United Steelworkers of America, the Yukon Government, ourselves, and the management of Cyprus Anvil. Up to the present time there has been an all-party type of agreement to put forward an action plan which I could take to my colleagues in Cabinet for approval. subsubtopic: MR. GURBIN-SHIFT IN MANUFACTURERS' SALES TAX
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I would like to present a petition on behalf of residents of Ontario, many of whom reside in my constituency of Bruce-Grey.
At a time when Canadians face serious economic distress, inflation runs rampant and governments' share of the gross national product is approximately 45 per cent-higher than at any time since World War II-it is inappropriate for additional taxation of several billions of dollars to be imposed. Notwithstanding the Minister of Finance's recent deferral and in response to his stated desire for further assessment with possible future imposition, on behalf of Canadian businessmen and consumers this petition requests the Government to cancel the proposal to shift the federal sales tax from the manufacturing to the wholesale level.

subsubtopic: MR. RIIS-CALL FOR GENERAL ELECTION
speechtext: Madam Speaker, I have the privilege today of presenting to the House a petition signed by nearly 2,000 constituents who are so concerned about the state of the Canadian economy that they are asking Parliament to urge the Prime Minister of Canada (Mr. Trudeau) to ask the Governor General for the dissolution of Parliament in order that a general election may be held.

November 2, 1982

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: I have notice of a request for a debate under Standing Order 26 from the Hon. Member for Portage-Marquette (Mr. Mayer).

Madam Speaker, I seek leave to move the adjournment of the House under the provisions of Standing Order 26, seconded by the Hon. Member for Kindersley-Lloydminster (Mr. McKnight), to debate a specific and important matter which I believe all Canadians would agree requires immediate consideration, namely, the work stoppage at the Port of Vancouver and at other ports on the west coast.
Since October 19 this work stoppage has had, and continues to have, a serious and negative effect on the total Canadian economy; it is not simply isolated to the west coast. The Minister of Finance (Mr. Lalonde) said some six days ago that he intended to see that the ports on the west coast were operating today. We now know that the Government-or at least it appears so-does not intend to introduce legislation today. Thus the strike or the work stoppage will continue. Last Friday the Finance Minister said that he would move quickly to see that the work stoppage is concluded.
This truly is a national emergency. Our national institution is Parliament. I urge you, Madam Speaker, to recognize that it is a national emergency and that Parliament be allowed to address this very important issue. I separate Parliament and the Government, in that we be allowed under the provisions of Standing Order 26 to use the parliamentary system to attempt to convince the Government that it should accept its responsibility to all Canadians to ensure that this very unfortunate and foolish work stoppage on the west coast ceases. Both parties, labour and management, are purported to have said that they would accept back-to-work legislation.
In conclusion, Madam Speaker, if you find this application for a debate acceptable, I would be very pleased to move the appropriate motion at the appropriate time.
Hear, hear!

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext:
Of course, the House will recall that I had a similar request on Thursday, October 28, and that at that time I came to the conclusion that in spite of the obvious importance of the impact of this particular situation on the country, I could not allow an emergency debate under Standing Order 26 because there was an opportunity to discuss this question under the different proceedings taking place in the House.
Those circumstances have not changed. As a matter of fact, they are quite similar. This afternoon we will be discussing the borrowing Bill, and Hon. Members know that yesterday they could have discussed the question in the course of the day reserved for the Opposition. Also there will be on next Friday another supply day set aside so that the Opposition may take the opportunity to discuss that particular question. We all know that some legislation is impending.
Therefore, I cannot escape the conclusion that there was an opportunity yesterday and that there will be an opportunity tomorrow and this afternoon to discuss this particular matter. I remind Hon. Members that the Chair is concerned with the urgency of the debate, not at all with the substance of the matter or the urgency of a settlement in the matter. Only the urgency of the debate concerns the Chair. Obviously Hon. Members will be able to debate the question. I am sorry to say that under the circumstances I cannot allow an emergency debate on this very important matter today.

subtopic: SUPPLEMENTARY BORROWING AUTHORITY ACT, 1982-83 (NO. 2) MEASURE TO ESTABLISH

speechtext: The House resumed, from Friday, October 29, consideration of the motion of Mr. Cosgrove (for the Minister of Finance) that Bill C-128, to provide supplementary borrowing authority (No. 2), be read the second time and referred to a Committee of the Whole.

subtopic: SUPPLEMENTARY BORROWING AUTHORITY ACT, 1982-83 (NO. 2) MEASURE TO ESTABLISH
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, it is a pleasure for me to resume the debate on the borrowing authority Bill which was introduced by the Minister of Finance (Mr. Lalonde) at the time of the presentation of his financial statement. Just prior to ending my remarks on Friday, I was indicating that there was a definite procedure and process being followed by the Government in the discussion by the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) with the people on television, moving to the financial statement of the Minister of Finance to set the stage, give the people the facts and put the information before them.
That would then be followed, of course, by a Speech from the Throne which would set the general policy thrust of the Government over the coming session of Parliament. That would be followed, as the Minister of Finance has already indicated, by a budget very early on in the new year to set forward specific policies implementing the policy thrust set out in the Speech from the Throne.
When I concluded those remarks last Friday I then proceeded to analyse some ideas that were placed before this House during this period of debate on the borrowing authority bill. Specifically, I was very interested in the comments put forward by the Leader of the New Democratic Party (Mr. Broadbent). Apart from the issues put forward by the Minister of Finance in his financial statement, they are really the only concrete alternative proposals put forward by the Opposition Parties concerning other policy prescriptions which could be followed by Government and which might provide some relief and respite for the Canadian people. I had intended to discuss these points very briefly in an objective way, trying to be nonpartisan in analysing what it was the Leader of the New Democratic Party had put forward. I had intended to look at these from the perspective of their potential to resolve the problems facing the country today.
I will do that now in two ways. First is the proposal that the Government should introduce new job creation to the extent of $2.2 billion, to be financed by raising the taxes of the so-called rich, and also by cutting expenditures in other areas, if I am not mistaken. Some of those areas were laid out by the Leader of the New Democratic Party.
November 2, 1982

In my reading of tax policy and the financial figures over the last several years, the amount of money that it was indicated would be available from a tax on the rich was, I believe, $1.1 billion, if all people earning over $40,000 per year were subjected to a 5 per cent surtax. As the Minister of Finance has pointed out, my analysis of the figures indicates that those figures are quite high. I would think that an order of magnitude of half of that is what is possible, although I would like to see the figures before I make a final judgment.

Mr. Speaker, six months ago I moved to this seat.
My point of order concerns a point which the Hon. Member was making involving a surtax which the New Democratic Party has suggested be placed on individual income earners receiving in excess of $40,000. We suggested that a 2 per cent surtax to be placed on those making $40,000 to $50,000 annually be graduated upwards so that people making $200,000 plus would be paying 9 per cent additional tax. Perhaps the Hon. Member in his calculations has not allowed for this graduated increase and that is why his figures differ somewhat from my leader's.

subtopic: SUPPLEMENTARY BORROWING AUTHORITY ACT, 1982-83 (NO. 2) MEASURE TO ESTABLISH
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I thank the Hon. Member for Kamloops-Shuswap (Mr. Riis) for the clarification he has just made. I will factor the information into my calculations. Moving up the income scale, the number of people affected obviously declines dramatically as income rises. If, in fact, that balancing of 2 per cent on $40,000 to $50,000, increasing to 9 per cent, is correct, I would expect that rather than increasing the volume of revenue it would actually decrease the volume of revenue. However, I will check into that and talk to the Hon. Member for Kamloops-Shuswap on that point.
Some analysis has been made to the effect that if the Government were to tax every dime of income over $30,000 in this country, in any one year it would amount to somewhere in the range of $400 per man, woman and child. If we are talking about taxing the rich to solve all our problems that, I am afraid, is illusory. I am afraid that kind of policy would cut off incentive and entrepreneurship completely, which would mean that the revenue expected probably could not be realized.
More importantly, even if you impose a 100 per cent surtax on everything over $30,000, the amount you would get is about $400 per man, woman and child. Therefore, there is not that much revenue to be had, contrary to the point put forward and
Supplementary Borrowing Authority
what some would have us believe about the vast wealth, in terms of income flow in any one year, of those who are termed to be rich.
Another interesting point that was raised by the Leader of the New Democratic Party concerned a new kind of industrial policy which would be put forward. This concept is quite new for the New Democratic Party; certain firms chosen to be the industries of the future-I think that is putting it fairly- would receive tax breaks. In other words, those firms would pay a lower tax rate than the general corporate citizens in our country and all of those who are not considered to be industries of the future or industries that generate long-term, good jobs for Canadians would be subject to the equivalent of a surtax. Their tax would rise. The rate would go from 36 per cent federal to 46 per cent or 48 per cent federal, and if you factor in both federal and provincial taxes, a tax rate of about 62 per cent or 63 per cent would result on all of those corporations not deemed to be industries of the future; that is not worthly of encouragement.
I can guarantee that many of those firms that we are talking about as those that might not be the big firms or the potential firms of the future are indeed the high labour content firms. They are the pulp and paper firms, the footwear firms, the textile firms, perhaps firms in the automobile industry and firms in some other industries which have a very high labour-to-capital ratio.
The Leader of the New Democratic Party is saying that his party would increase taxes on firms with a very high labour content. As a result of having a high labour content in a country with high wage rates relative to some underdeveloped countries, these firms would be on the decline in Canada. The number of capital intensive firms would be on the rise in Canada and the number of labour intensive firms would tend to be on the decline because of competition from low labour cost firms in low labour cost countries. Therefore, increasing the tax rate on those firms which now employ a large number of people would simply speed up the process of their demise. This would result in a great many people being thrown out of work in order to encourage another group of firms that would probably be more capital intensive in nature. Perhaps not, but at least they would be more capital intensive than the firms being penalized by the higher tax rate. That to me indicates an interesting change of strategy from the point of view of what has traditionally been the position of the New Democratic Party.
There is another point on this particular topic that I would like to discuss. In the past this Party, our Government, has been criticized very strongly for introducing what the Hon. Member for Oshawa has called loopholes, which are nothing more than tax incentives to encourage firms to invest and create jobs in the traditional sense. I think Hon. Members from the Conservative Party are agreeing, nodding their heads, smiling and looking for more.

subtopic: SUPPLEMENTARY BORROWING AUTHORITY ACT, 1982-83 (NO. 2) MEASURE TO ESTABLISH
speechtext:
The point is that the appropriateness of providing selective incentives has been a contentious issue among Members in the House of different Parties. Personally, I do not like selective incentives. I think that it is more appropriate to have lower tax rates than selective incentives. However, we are not discussing that argument at this point.
Let us consider the incentive issue. The New Democratic Party has traditionally been opposed to selective incentives which would reward firms. That has not been a traditional position, as far as I know. However, we now find that their position has changed. Objectively speaking, it appears that there has been a rather dramatic change in policy which effectively proposes that incentives will be given to the firms which have the greatest probability of success in the future.
Incentives given to innovative and creative firms seem to me like reverse welfare. Who will be paying the heavier taxes? It will be those firms on their way out and that do not have a great future. Who will benefit from these incentives? It will be the firms which do have a great future and which have an opportunity to make a great deal of money and generate a great deal of wealth. It seems to me that we are talking about taking form the poor to give to the rich at the corporate level. That is not a policy which has traditionally been held by the New Democratic Party.
Apparently what is being requested is a replacement of those tax incentives which have traditionally been accepted by the Liberal Party or the Conservative Party, when it was in power, by those types of tax incentives which now happen to be in favour with the New Democratic Party. There does not seem to be any great difference in policy or philosophy in this case. It is simply a matter of deciding which firms with the greatest future will be rewarded with tax incentives. That seems to be the thrust of their suggestion.

speechtext:
There is no disrespect intended, Mr. Speaker.
I believe that it is beneficial to debate what is being proposed by other Members in the House of Commons. The Hon. Member for Oshawa, the Leader of the New Democratic Party, put forward some proposals. I have given my reaction to those proposals and I hope that other Members will feel free to give their reaction also, just as they feel free to comment on the proposals and decisions made by the Minister of Finance in his recent financial statement. I hope that some Members of the Conservative Party will introduce some positive proposals that can be analysed and debated in the House in this same manner.
Before I discuss some points which I think are important about the statement by the Minister of Finance, I must first give credit to the previous Minister of Finance, the Hon. Member for Cape Breton Highlands-Canso (Mr. MacEachen), for the changes which he brought about in the green paper on the budgetary process. He has made this process more open and has provided for consultation on economic policies to a much greater extent than has ever taken place before. This greater consultation has been taking place during his tenure and is being continued very successfully by the current Minister of Finance. I believe that the former Minister of Finance has done a great thing for Parliament and for Government by introducing a much more open process. I suggest that history will thank him for introducing those innovations in the budgetary process and for improving the consultative environment which we have seen taking place. That environment has dramatically improved in the last year, and in recent months in particular.
I was most pleased with the Minister of Finance's introductory remarks on page 3 of his statement which dealt with the basic principles of economic management which he indicated he intended to follow as Minister of Finance. When one reads and understands the six principles laid out by the Minister in his statement, I believe that Canadians and Members of Parliament will be able clearly to understand his intentions, his priorities and what we may expect from him in the future.
I acknowledge that we have a terrible unemployment problem in Canada. While we must give our utmost attention to this extremely serious dilemma, we must acknowledge that some progress is certainly being made on other fronts. For example, declining inflation surely must be a positive sign for the investment climate and for consumer confidence in this
November 2, 1982

country. The annualized year over year rate is 10.4 per cent, which is down considerably from what it was in earlier months. More importantly, when one considers inflation during the last three months, one sees that the annualized rate of inflation for the three-month period of July, August and September in Canada is 6.6 per cent. This downward trend has been continuing for some time now. It represents great progress and I believe it is reason for us to have some confidence that we have, in fact, finally got a grip on the inflation problem. I suggest we will see even greater progress in the future.
The fact that interest rates have dropped dramatically indicates that the market agrees with this assessment. In fact, interest rates have dropped for 11 consecutive weeks and we hope they will continue to drop in the coming weeks. That assessment of the market shows that Government action and market actions generally are in the process of bringing inflation under control in Canada. It must certainly be seen as a very positive sign.
However, that does not let us ignore the fact that we have a very serious unemployment problem and that we must deal with the fundamentals of that problem. Certainly we must make funds available for job creation in the short term in order to help those unemployed during this very difficult transition period. But the ultimate solution to the unemployment problem will result from improvements in the investment climate, the economic structure and world markets. It is fallacious and cruel to suggest to Canadians that Government action alone, whether Liberal, Conservative, NDP or Social Credit, could eradicate the unemployment problem by a simple wave of a magic wand. That will not happen. The unemployment problem will be with us for some time to come. Governments by themselves will not be able to solve the problem. This includes federal, provincial and municipal Governments.
The unemployment problem must be solved through a regeneration of growth and prosperity within the economy generally and a regeneration of growth and prosperity outside of Canada where the markets are for the vast resources that we mine and mill for sale elsewhere. The markets for the forest products industry, the mining industry and the pulp and paper industry are not primarily here in Canada. Those are export products. When our export markets are down, when other countries are not buying our goods, it makes absolutely no sense to follow the suggestion that we subsidize continued production and stockpile, building inventories that cost money. It costs money to produce, the money would have to be borrowed, and the interest charges on the borrowed money would certainly add to the cost burden of government which is shared and carried by the taxpayers. That kind of policy would mean vast stockpiling of produced goods that we could sell abroad, but when the markets do recover the people who were working at that point would not have to work because we would be able to sell from our vast inventories. Stockpiling large quantities of raw materials would simply mean that the kind of employment recovery which comes along with a general economic recovery
Supplementary Borrowing Authority
would not happen because we would have vast inventories from which we could sell to the market for years to come.
It does not seem to be a very innovative or realistic policy because all we would be doing would be easing some of the unemployment burden today and shifting it into the future. Certainly those people who are working in the mines in two or three years from now would have to contend with the existence of these huge inventories. It would be a very dangerous strategy to subsidize miners and forest workers to produce goods, for which there is no current market, in anticipation that such market would appear once again at some time in the future, as suggested by some Hon. Members. It is simply not a strategy which is realistic at this time.
I believe our unemployment problem will be long-term. We will have to contend with it, not so much by trying to keep people at work in existing jobs where there are rising questions as to the future viability of the industries for which they work, but rather, by looking further than that and considering new skills programs, such as that brought forward several months ago by the Hon. Minister of Employment and Immigration (Mr. Axworthy).
We must ask ourselves, "Where is the future for employment in this country? How can we move people from industries where the future simply does not exist for Canada?" It may exist for some southeast Asian country which has very low labour costs, or for a South American country, but it certainly does not exist for a country such as Canada with relatively high labour costs. We must look to those industries and ask ourselves how we can help the people working in those industries to move to other industries which have a comparative advantage for Canada. That will not be done by Government alone. There will not be a situation where the Government can state: "These are the cities of the future; this is where we will put all the money". It does not seem that that proposition would be valid.
I am not being in any way derogatory of my colleagues in the House or my friends who work in the Public Service who have some great insight as to where the future lies. If the Government were to take on the role and responsibility of defining where the prosperous future lies, it would place great risks on the backs of the taxpayers. I think the marketplace has performed that function very well in the past.
Government should act as a catalytic agent to assist the market in moving people from where the jobs are declining to areas where they are increasing. I believe we can do this through labour, management and Government task forces which would give us a better view as to where our skills and training programs should be focused. We could do it that way, but I would be very reluctant to see the Government go it alone and try to define what the future will be. Those governments, whether they be federal, provincial, Canadian or foreign, which have tried that kind of approach in the past have generally wound up in a very dismal state within a few years. They have certainly picked some winners, but over time

they have picked many more losers, and those losers have become a great portfolio which the taxpayers must drag along with them into the future. Quite frankly, I do not believe that is the way to go.
Members of Parliament are all very well intentioned and none of us has a corner on virtue or on a desire to help our constituents. Everyone is in the House because they want to help their constituents. They want to see the country grow, one which is better when they depart from public office than the one they inherited when they came into public office. I think all of us feel that way. To a large extent, I think we are doing ourselves a great disservice in the House from time to time because we carry on debate in a fashion which tends to be very partisan and rhetorical in an attempt to score political points. That kind of approach leads to an attitude on the part of our constituents that we are not behaving like adults. I do not believe there is one of us here who has not come back from the summer recess with the knowledge that constituents are asking, "What in the world are you doing in that House of Commons? You are not dealing with the serious problems that are crushing us. We want to see you behave in a diplomatic and statesmanlike fashion and come to grips with the problems in an objective way."
That is what we must do in this House of Commons. It is unrealistic and is misleading Canadians when they view Members who stand up in the House and say they have all the answers, and then provide a pie in the sky solution to the problems with which Canadians are grappling in their own lives, or build up hope that there is some kind of magic fairy godmother called Government which will come along and wave the magic wand and unemployment will disappear overnight.
Some Members say: "If only we were in power, Government would be so much more efficient and the problems would evaporate overnight". I do not mean that in a partisan sense. The fact is that no matter who is in power, the problems with us are real, fundamental and deeply rooted, and we will have to go through a period of very hard work as Parliamentarians and as a country in order to pull oursleves out of this situation.
That is precisely the message the Prime Minister was trying to deliver. He was not trying to put forward specific policy recommendations in his three evening speeches. He was trying to say that if we do not start to co-operate here in the House of Commons and, more generally, across the country, if we do not start to see some co-operation between Government and management, then we will not pull ourselves out of this situation. I would ask Hon. Members in the New Democratic Party, who probably have a much closer relationship with the labour movement than the other two major parties, to sit down with their colleagues at the leadership level of the labour movement to try to establish a more co-operative framework for discussion and dialogue.
We should try to develop the kind of national economic policy consensus whereby we can come together as Canadians, moving forward and taking the very hard, very real decisions which must be taken if we are to move into a period of rising
living standards in the future. We should do that co-operatively, without the kind of animosity, anger and vitriol which has characterized discussions between those three centres of power in our country in the past. I would ask that all Members of Parliament join together in the committees and in the House to see if we cannot come together in a more co-operative, nonpartisan environment to deal with the fundamental problems of this country on behalf of Canadians, as we were elected to do.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in listening to the words of the Hon. Member for Ottawa Centre (Mr. Evans), I found that in some respects he tried to follow the same line as that taken by his leader, the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau), during his television speech some nights ago. He was trying to reassure the Canadian public that if we all work together, pull together, things will be better in the future. The one thing that most Members of Parliament found this summer in their constituencies-and if they do not admit it publicly, I suggest they do privately-is the one universal fact that most people realize that we are in a very serious economic situation, probably the worst recession since the Great Depression in the 1930s, and that there is no way, regardless of what political party is in power at this time, that we could have gotten out of the problem. In fact, Canada would not have escaped for a whole series of reasons, most of them well known to everyone.
However, what grates on most Canadians, certainly those in my constituency in southern Manitoba and, I suggest, in other constituencies as well, is the fact that the problem to an extent is of our own making through basically stupid Government policies over the last number of years, policies that have exacerbated the problem.
This is something, Mr. Speaker, that I do not think people are going to forget. It would be great if we could wipe the slate clean and say that it is all behind us now and we will march off in the sunset together to form a great nation. But people do not think that way and governments and countries do not work that way. I hope in my few short remarks I can demonstrate some of the problems that have brought us into this whole situation. There are some things very dear to many Canadian hearts, like the National Energy Program or the Foreign Investment Review Act. There has been a series of economic moves that have made us far worse off today than we were before.
Just how bad are things in Canada? We have a national unemployment rate that has reached a record 12.2 per cent which reflects the fact that 1,343,000 Canadians are out of work. In additon, 338,000 Canadians are working part-time because they cannot find full-time employment. The unemployment totals do not include the 96,000 people that are classified as discouraged workers, who have given up even looking for work because there are just no jobs available. I think we in the House of Commons are very fortunate to have jobs, although they may not all be that secure. Nevertheless, it is difficult for us to imagine the kind of frustration men and
November 2, 1982

women at all levels of the labour force feel who find themselves out of work, when they have nothing to get up for in the morning, to look forward to. They have to depend on the Government through unemployment insurance to buy necessities; and as we get closer to Christmas, you cannot turn a television on without advertisements to buy newer, better, bigger things. That kind of human misery is incalculable.
In 1981 there were over 8,000 business bankruptcies across the country. Bankruptcies in 1981 were 22 per cent higher than in 1980 and 43 per cent higher than in 1979. We can see the kind of acceleration that is taking place there and it is going to get worse. Rural ridings right across the country are in a critical situation. In my own rural riding in southern Manitoba the agricultural community, which is by far the largest group in my constituency and the largest part of the activity generated in Manitoba, was hit with interest rates which nobody could understand or deal with. That, Mr. Speaker, coupled with the fact that we have agricultural prices generally across the board that in real terms are almost at depression levels, has caused hardships of a kind that I have not seen in southern Manitoba in many, many years. Of course, the communities in the rural parts of Canada are there because agriculture is there. If agriculture suffers, the communities, and the small businessmen who provide the services, suffer even worse.
As an example, corn is grown in large quantities now in Manitoba, parts of Ontario and Quebec. Last year prices were in the neighbourhood of $3.30-$3.40 a bushel. Now the price is $2.10 a bushel. It usually takes $2.50 a bushel to get your investment back. That is the kind of loss that agriculture is facing, and that is reflected throughout the whole food industry. The situation is more serious than it has ever been. That is not necessarily the fault of the Government. It is the fault of a large, world-wide grain crop, certainly in the United States and North America, that has not moved to market at the present time and does not look as if it will in the future. This double slap in the face to this segment of the population, of course, is causing all kinds of problems.
In the second quarter of 1982, Canadian manufacturers were operating at only 68 per cent of total capacity. That means, Mr. Speaker, some 32 per cent of the capacity in this country is sitting idle because of the kind of economic recession which has taken place. No wonder we have over one million Canadians out of work.
The value of building permits, as most people know, were down substantially in July, 1982 by 38 per cent compared to July of 1981. If inflation is taken into account, building activity is down almost 50 per cent over last year. The purchasing power of the 1971 dollar is now 37 cents; consumers, particularly housewives, know that the purchasing power of the dollar is down.
Part of our very serious situation has been brought on because of other economic factors which have taken place around the world, generally overspending by all levels of government in other countries. But that is only a portion of the Canadian problem because we have the situation where we

find ourselves with a Liberal Government which has been almost continuously in power over the last decade and which has caused the problem to accelerate.
The Government is asking the country for permission to borrow another $4 billion. The Minister of Finance (Mr. Lalonde) stated that total spending this year would be approximately $80 billion, $23.6 billion more than the Government will take in through revenues. He has even admitted that further borrowing authority may be required before the end of the fiscal year.
Let us translate that for ourselves as that is the only way that most Canadians can understand what is happening. It is very difficult to grasp the meaning of a figure as large as that. Eighty billion dollars is a lot of money. We know that if individually we spent more money than we took in, such as through our salary, we would all go broke. That is what appears to be happening. It appears that this country is going broke. We have a situation in which money is being borrowed to pay interest on money borrowed previously. Taken to its logical conclusion, it creates a frightening scenario.
In my opinion, there are at least four definite economic costs of continued deficit financing of the magnitude being pursued by the present Government. First, there is the ever growing interest burden. Interest on the debt this year will amount to $18 billion, the equivalent of about $700 for every man, woman and child in Canada or about $1,700 per taxpayer. That means that about one dollar in every three is being paid to the Government by taxpayers to service the national debt. For a family of four, that amounts to $2,800. That is what our national debt is costing us. It means there has been too much spending, too reckless spending, over a long period of time.
The second cost is a loss of fiscal flexibility. In the past, the Government had the option of undertaking costly and significant fiscal measures to spur the economy. Today there is no room to manoeuvre. We are locked in and can do very little. Literally all that can be done is what the Minister of Finance did the other night. It is the old shell game, moving the money around. It is trying to plug some small hole in the dike. I repeat, there is no room to manoeuvre. Unemployment, and the misery associated with it, will get worse in the coming winter.
The third cost is that productive private sector borrowing is crowded out and, consequently, interest rates rise. In the 1981 calendar year, federal Government borrowing accounted for about 44 per cent of the net new security issues placed in Canada. The figure this year will be higher. If there was less federal Government borrowing, there would be less demand for money and hence interest rates would be lower. Because of the tremendous demand created by federal Government borrowing in competition with other sectors, there is a tendency for interest rates possibly, but hopefully not, to start to rise again in the future. We have never had the magnitude of Government borrowing that we have at the present time.

The fourth cost is that of confidence. Possibly this is the toughest cost to overcome. The investment community do not trust a Government that continues to live so far beyond its means. They do not want to hold a currency that continues to be debased by excessive Government borrowing. As a consequence, the dollar has fallen, driving up the cost of living in Canada. Interest rates remain high as the Government attempts to support the dollar. Job-creating investment has gone elsewhere. Capital investment has gone elsewhere.
These are some of the economic costs of the deficit financing that Canadians are experiencing at the present time. In his recent economic statement, the Minister of Finance proposed to reallocate expenditures of $1.1 billion into several job-creating schemes, an exercise he called very difficult. If the Liberal Government had behaved in a financially responsible way for the last decade-and it has been in power almost continually in that period of time-there would be no need to borrow another $4 billion, no need to announce mere band-aid, job stimulation measures. That is not to say we would not be in a recession, that we would not be in trouble in terms of manufacturing or have the idle plant capacity I talked about, but we would not be in the present situation.
If wasteful Government spending had instead been used to encourage productivity, promote research and development and help place Canada on a more competitive footing with our foreign trading rivals, Canadians would not be suffering as much as they are today from the worst economic climate since the Great Depression. It is because of the billions of dollars wasted by this Government that the Liberals are here today in the House looking for more money. The money wasted could have been used to produce many stimulative and varied proposals. I would like to mention two or three in my remarks.
Early in the fall of 1981, the then Minister of Finance set an interest rate of 19.5 per cent on that year's offering of Canada Savings Bonds. To compound the mistake, he was obliged to offer the same rate to existing bond holders to prevent a wave of conversion from old bonds to new. Obviously the interest rate was very attractive. Soon after the offering was made, it became obvious that interest rates were declining and that the Government could easily have borrowed all it wanted at around 15 per cent.
This absurd blunder left Canadian taxpayers burdened with $25 billion in Savings Bonds debt at 19.5 per cent interest for a full year. The estimated cost of the interest alone was in the area of $4.9 billion. Because of a rash decision by the then Minister of Finance, at least $1 billion was wasted in paying inflationary and unnecessarily high interest rates.
In February, 1981 the federal Government purchased Petrofina for about $1.46 billion, or $120 per share. At the time of the purchase the shares were trading at about $90 per share. In other words, the federal Government paid between $365 million and $486 million more than was necessary.
To date spending by the federal Government on the metric conversion program exceeds some $65 million. Ever since metric conversion was first talked about, many people have felt it was a totally unnecessary expense. The Government has an advertising and information budget to get its programs across to the people of Canada in addition to the advertising being
done by the various Departments, which amounts to $235 million, the largest advertising budget in Canada. This money is used to promote its image. That is another expenditure which is considered needless. Nevertheless, some people will say it is only $235 million. The $235 millions all add up, Mr. Speaker, to a substantial amount of money.
It is no wonder that Canadians doubt the Prime Minister and question his sincerity when he goes on television three nights in a row to say, in effect, "Let us forget the past; let us join hands, pull together and move forward". They say: "Where were you the last few years? You have destroyed your credibility. We do not believe you any more." That element so important in politics, that which is probably everything in politics, the element called trust, is not there any more. When you do not have that element of trust it is very difficult to govern, to be a Prime Minister, to be in Opposition, or to be a politician at whatever level.
As to the indecisiveness we are seeing at the present time, I think that can be demonstrated in no better way than by the grain transportation shutdown on the west coast. Everyone in this House agreed that when that took place there should be a certain time limit allowed to see whether the parties could get together. But it has become more than apparent to everyone involved that the whole process was a charade. There have not been any real and meaningful negotiations probably for the last nine months. Why? Because both sides have the safety net of the House of Commons to solve the problem for them and they are going to use it.
As to being decisive, why have we waited so long to solve their problem if in fact we have to? In my opinion, Mr. Speaker, we should have dealt with the Bill last Friday afternoon. That was the absolute latest we should have allowed this strike to carry on. The weekend could have been used to get the workers back to work and grain and other very vital exports moving through the Port of Vancouver. Of course, that has not happened. Today is Tuesday and we are going to deal with it, hopefully, on Wednesday. We have not seen the Bill yet, although it may be and probably is drafted and ready to be presented.
It is that kind of indecision which, once again, breeds distrust. You cannot have it both ways. You cannot go on television and ask for the trust of the Canadian people and at the same time be so indecisive and, as an Hon. Member said, break your word on bringing in legislation which affects a very large segment of this country. In fact, this situation is blocking the only major export we have at the present time, the only product where we can compete with anyone anywhere in the world, that of grain and oil seeds moving out of this country.
To conclude my remarks, Mr. Speaker, the economic recovery will come, but unfortunately I think it is going to be very weak. It is going to have only a very moderate impact on our current fiscal and financial problems and that is going to
November 2, 1982

be too bad. In my opinion, broadly speaking there has to be a meaningful effort by Government-and by that I mean all of us here-to regain the confidence of the Canadian people which we have lost over the last number of years. Until we can do that, we are really going to be just shooting in the dark in terms of any policies we put forth in this House. Because, ultimately, the people have to believe that yes, the politicians are being sincere and honest in what they are trying to do. Until that happens, Mr. Speaker, I suggest that anything the Prime Minister, his cabinet or Government does will be met with the same kind of skepticism that the Prime Minister's speech was met with the other night.
Trust has to be built up and quickly. There have to be some dramatic moves in order to do that, coupled with-and unfortunately this will not take place, in my opinion, for 12 to 18 months-a strong and agressive economic recovery around the world with Canada moving in step with that recovery. The unfortunate reality we are faced with right now is that we as a Government are going to muddle around for the next 12 to 18 months, until the middle of 1984, before things start to get on track. It is going to be tough on Canadians, tough on workers and on business. It will be very tough on politicians and our institutions at all levels. But, Mr. Speaker, if we all work together, possibly we can overcome some of this.
I can say one thing. I know people certainly in my part of the country are looking very longingly at starting to overcome some of these problems at the next federal election. There is no way that the Liberal Party will govern this country again through the middle part of the 1980s. The trust is gone and it will not come back that quickly.

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I wonder if the Hon. Member for Lisgar (Mr. Murta) would entertain a question. He mentioned in his remarks something about getting the workers in the port of Vancouver back to work. I wonder if he would change that comment in view of the fact that it is a lock-out, not a strike, and also that the workers have been ready to go back to work. Indeed, I am not sure the public realizes, in particular that part of the public from his part of Canada, that the employers themselves have not made arrangements to have the grain shipments continue, which the union was willing to do.

Mr. Speaker, I will make the required change. It is a lock-out. The unfortunate problem is that when we do have a lock-out, as we have at the present time in Vancouver, we have a tendency to view it as if the workers were going out on strike and management is, in effect, sitting back with clean hands. Of course, that is not the case.
I will not argue the question of who is to blame in this particular instance because I think that is pointless. However, I would say that as long as Parliament acts as a safety net for both parties to this dispute to fall back into, we are not going to have any kind of meaningful bargaining in the future. So I think we have to come to some kind of decision about whether or not we are going to make some of these areas possibly essential services and do what we have to do to ensure that the
Supplementary Borrowing Authority
stoppage does not continue. In my opinion there has to be a decision made somewhere, Mr. Speaker, otherwise we will find Parliament continuing to be the arbitrator for these disputes. If we could afford the luxury it would be great to leave the whole thing alone until the parties settle their own problems; but Canada cannot afford that luxury. I do not know whether we will get to that at this point in time. I doubt it, because we never do.
Certainly it would not be a bad idea for some body, if not a parliamentary group then some other group in the country, to take a hard look at whether the movement of commodities going through a port like Vancouver-commodities that literally cannot be held up regardless of whether that be by Government, management or labour-should be designated as an essential service to this country that ought not to be interfered with, and whether binding arbitration, back-to-work legislation or some other action is necessary.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to be able to participate in the debate today, particularly in view of the present economic situation in Canada. Since last Wednesday we have heard many comments, much criticism and many suggestions, both in this House and throughout the country, but all in all, the general impression we have received was one of favourable reaction to last week's financial statement by the Minister of Finance. I think all Canadians have understood, and one would wish that was also the case in the House, that the present recession affecting Canada and many other countries-in fact, I could even say most countries cannot be blamed entirely on this government's administration. We all know that the economic problems besetting France, the United States, Great Britain, West Germany and even Japan are also affecting our country. The fact that the American steel industry had to cut production by 40 per cent last year, which was now led to the closing down of the town of Scheffer-ville, as announced today, cannot be blamed solely on the Canadian government. Our steel producers had to go along with what was happening in the United States. However, realizing that the situation was becoming extremely difficult for these people, the government had already taken action well before this shutdown by designating the region, and today, once more, the Minister of Employment and Immigration has taken decisive action and delegated as of this afternoon a number of officials to this particular area in Quebec, to meet with company management and with company employees and see what should be done to deal as quickly as possible with the problems facing these employees in Northwestern Quebec.
On the other hand, Mr. Speaker, the economy is expected to improve in the months to come, and in any case some time next year. Last week, the Conference Board of Canada announced that our gross national product is on the rise, that

inflation is expected to go down and has already started to do so and that interest rates are dropping. So of course, all this will have its effect on the country. Granted, the situation is not a pleasant one, and of course we would prefer inflation and interest rates to go down more rapidly, but still, the government had already anticipated the situation and injected $1.4 billion in direct job creation. These projects, including community development programs, are already in place and in January and February, 60,000 jobs will be created in Canada under these programs.
You know, I was listening in the House, yesterday and again today, during question period and during the debate when a number of members were explaining that people in various parts of the country had specific problems. Mr. Speaker, I would like to remind you that $ 1.4 billion was injected into the Canadian economy to provide jobs for a large number of workers, part of those funds going to two provinces that have been more severely affected than others, namely Ontario and British Columbia. Last year, for instance, Ontario received $16 million for these job creation programs. However, because of the difficult economic situation, this year funding was increased to $29.5 million, or twice the amount invested last year. And in British Columbia, where last year only $6 million were injected into these programs, this year the department and the Government of Canada are providing $15,5 million to fund these programs. Thus, the government had anticipated the situation and set aside substantial amounts for these provinces, especially in areas where a high unemployment rate was expected as a result of factory shutdowns and where many people would need help. Mr. Speaker, Quebec has also had its share of job creation programs, because we are aware that this province has one of the highest unemployment rates in Canada. Last year, we put $48 million into job creation programs and this year that amount was raised to $72.5 million.
In addition, the Department of Employment and Immigration set aside $41 million for very urgent cases, because we anticipated that some regions, without necessarily knowing which ones, would be faced with very pressing problems. That is why the Minister of Employment and Immigration (Mr. Axworthy) asked his officials in June and July of this year to find out where the number of shutdowns would be highest and where people would be most likely to exhaust their unemployment insurance benefits. The report was published a month ago, and we have started allocating the $41 million fund throughout Canada so that workers who, in another four to five weeks, may be faced with the choice of going on welfare or looking for another job will be able to take advantage of these measures. The department is in the final stages of allocating the funds on the basis of the information it has been given. In the Province of Quebec alone, the department has allocated $9.4 million of the $41 million fund to meet specific needs in certain regions.
In October, I was in Quebec City with some of my colleagues when the present Minister of National Revenue (Mr. Bussieres) announced that $1.3 million would be going to that city alone to meet its needs, in addition to the $2.8 million which the same region had received in July. The same applies to the Eastern Townships, which this past summer probably experienced more shutdowns than anywhere else in Quebec, had the largest increase in people drawing unemployment insurance benefits and the largest number of people who in the months to come would exhaust their unemployment benefits. Last week, I was pleased to announce that $2.3 million will be allocated to these ridings in addition to funds already announced in connection with training programs. Mr. Speaker, I think we can say that these funds were available because the government was aware of the situation and had taken steps to provide for the difficult months ahead.
Once more, we have to live within this world economic environment, even if we are not entirely responsible for the economic problems now facing the world, including Canada. Canadians must realize that major changes are going on in the job world. Workers in certain industries will have to look to other career choices as a result of the technological changes occurring in this country today. To respond to these major developments, in July of last year the government passed the National Training Act. This legislation will help many workers to switch occupations and acquire the skills they need to cope with the major changes we are facing today.
Later on I hope to elaborate on this training program, Mr. Speaker. In any case, the Minister of Finance (Mr. Lalonde) also announced other measures aimed at meeting specific needs. I am thinking here of the funds injected into the construction industry, where many jobs will be available during this period, and also of the funds made available to Canadian National and to a western railway company. All this, however, is an immediate response to present needs. Departmental and government projections also anticipated that this winter would be a very difficult one, and that we would have to be able to respond quickly to the needs that will become apparent during this period. I feel that the $500 million announced for job creation is a very concrete response by the government to these needs.
The fact remains, Mr. Speaker, that the federal government alone cannot solve all the world's problems or Canada's. As part of the consultations he has been conducting, the Minister of Employment and Immigration (Mr. Axworthy) is in New Brunswick this afternoon to meet with his provincial counterpart. Yesterday he was in Halifax. Last week, the minister went out West, to Manitoba and Saskatchewan, and also to Quebec City, to discuss with the provincial governments how the provinces and municipal governments could join the federal government in an effort to expand funding for job creation.
November 2, 1982

We also appealed to the private sector, because it would be asking the impossible to expect a simple level of government to cope with what is expected to be a difficult period. In carrying out these consultations, we hope that all concerned will pull together and work towards the same goals. If we manage to inject another $500 million or more in job creation, people everywhere at the local level will benefit from this funding and be able to obtain the financial resources they need to get through the difficult winter months. Mr. Speaker, these consultations are absolutely necessary, and our colleagues opposite would do well to co-operate with this government and make constructive suggestions to help us focus all job creation programs on the same goal, which is to provide jobs for as many Canadians as possible. When people need jobs, we must set aside all political partisanship.
Mr. Speaker, I have been discussing the need for jobs, and I know what I am talking about. In my area, the unemployment rate goes up to 60 per cent during the winter. People come to my office looking for jobs, and job creation programs are going to help us to provide many families with the financial resources they need to get through this period. Our consultations are therefore absolutely necessary. It is very reassuring to see that the Government of Quebec has changed its approach in this respect and seems to be willing to set aside the political bias which has governed its actions since it came to power, and to respond to the needs of Quebeckers. Last week's meeting in Quebec City was extremely productive, and last Friday, officials at both government levels were looking at job creation programs and at the possibility of reaching an agreement or providing ways of finding jobs for the people who need them.
It is obvious that the municipalities will play an enormous part in this debate. Moreover, we have asked the co-operation of the various agencies, and once again, it is to be hoped that the Quebec Government will allow them, in consultation with the Provincial and Federal Governments, to see if it is possible to find some way to create jobs. Of course, the Right Hon. Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) in his talks on television last week appealed to all Canadians because we need their understanding and co-operation.
Once again, Mr. Speaker, some people tell us that the economic problems of Canada are the responsibility of this government. I gave a few examples of this a while ago. It is obviously impossible to attempt to solve all the economic problems in the world by finding solutions to our economic problems in Canada. We want now to deal with a major problem, namely job creation. The Federal Government has made a clear and determined commitment in this regard, as have most Provincial Governments, and the purpose of the consultations now going on and started last week is precisely to obtain the co-operation of as many people as possible, of all levels of Government and the private sector so that everyone in Canada will show the same commitment and create jobs for Canadians this winter.

Mr. Speaker, these consultations did not come about only last week. I believe that there have been other examples. This past year, most Provinces have signed agreements with the Federal Government in many areas. There is for instance work sharing, through which we were able to save tens of thousands of jobs throughout the country. Once more, the workers themselves showed the Canadian people that they were willing to share when faced with hardships. In various plants and industries, all kinds of people have accepted to work shorter hours and shorter days to enable their colleagues, their fellow workers, to keep their jobs. We have benefited from this experience because we have reinforced these various programs within our Department and tried to use them to meet present needs, and we shall certainly continue to do so.
In Quebec for instance, as of October 26, the Work Sharing Program had benefited 1,179 companies and 47,480 employees and avoided the lay-off of 21,900 Quebec workers. This is a clear example of co-operation, and I believe it is concrete evidence that people are able to understand and help each other when facing hardships. Mr. Speaker, I believe that we can multiply these examples of co-operation and consultation throughout the country. Last week, the Minister of Finance (Mr. Lalonde) gave another example of consultation by appointing economists to a special group with whom he will consult so as to make decisions which are realistic and which will enable us to meet our present needs. Mr. Speaker, I would like to note at this time another important aspect of the present situation as well as the extremely important role played by many workers throughout the country.
Naturally, in my capacity as Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Employment and Immigration, I have visited a great many employment centres throughout Canada in the past twelve months and I have met thousands of workers. We often hear members say in the House that they have people coming to their office to tell them about their employment problems and other difficulties. Mr. Speaker, it must be understood that all the people who work in our employment centres in Canada are on the job five days a week, and quite often on Saturdays and Sundays as well, because they are asked to work overtime to handle the large number of applications filed with our centres in the past year. Mr. Speaker, those people are on the front line, yet when we call on the various centres across Canada we never hear them complain and say to us that they simply cannot do everything we ask them to do. Mr. Speaker, they perform their work like professionals, rapidly and with outstanding efficiency.
I have met them, Mr. Speaker, and I have told many of them that they deserve our admiration for performing their duties right where the action is every day. That explains why this government agreed last summer to hire 1,200 additional employees to help the centres cope with the flood of applications. Needless to say, those employees have ready access to

November 2, 1982
Supplementary Borrowing Authority
the information facilities of the Department so that they can keep applicants well informed, and they are doing their best. Of course, Mr. Speaker, there is the odd delay here and there, but our employees are not necessarily responsible for that and more often than not the computers cannot keep up with the applications. There may have been human errors now and then, but it must be said that most of those people are doing an outstanding job.
Another thing worth mentioning, Mr. Speaker, is that our current unemployment insurance program is actually an economic cushion, something which we did not have in Canada during the notorious depression of the thirties, for instance. Last week, in this House, we heard the Minister of Finance (Mr. Lalonde) state that he had considerably increased unemployment insurance premiums, justifiably because our unemployment insurance scheme managed by employers and employees should be self-financed. The Government of Canada had to decide whether premiums would be substantially increased or whether it would make up the deficit, but since this is a self-financed scheme, as 1 said, the Government has chosen a middle-of-the-road course and granted an increase which will allow the unemployment insurance fund to continue to provide employment through the various above-mentioned programs so that employers and employees will not be seized by the throat and unable to pay.
Once again, the Government has taken the right direction. It has increased the premiums while making sure that employees and employers will be in a position to pay their share, and taking the necessary steps to allow the UI fund to continue to pay benefits because we should not forget, Mr. Speaker, that unemployment insurance is an insurance, that those who pay contributions are entitled to draw benefits and that as many Canadians as possible should benefit from it. Needless to say, Mr. Speaker, this fund has also enabled us as in the case of the work sharing program mentioned earlier to set up other programs which have been implemented during the past year. There are programs, for instance, established under Section 38 of the Unemployment Insurance Act, where unemployed workers can draw additional unemployment insurance benefits while doing work for the benefit of the community.
Under agreements covering the forestry industry which have been signed in British Columbia, Ontario, the Maritimes and Quebec, many forestry workers have been able to remain physically active and continue to work in the same sector. These agreements will also enable them to return quickly to the labour market as soon as the economy recovers. The federal government has approved $220 million for this program for the year 1982-1983. Mr. Speaker, in my area, in Eastern Quebec where forestry and fisheries are the main industries, we have signed similar agreements with thirteen non-profit enterprises, and at the same time we were also able to deal with a major problem, namely the spruce budworm epidemic. Thus we shall be able to safeguard our forests,
enable workers to go on working in their own field and help their families to get through the winter.
These programs have all been very well received by the workers. These are some of the possibilities we shall be looking into under our new job creation program. We shall be considering ways of improving or adapting the programs to make them more responsive to the real situation. These are some of the things we shall try to do in the weeks to come.
Mr. Speaker, perhaps I could say a few more words about our occupational training program to which I was referring earlier in my speech. This program is of course extremely important, as we are going to invest $1 billion in it this year alone. As I said before, we are going to help many workers in Canada acquire additional skills and help them retrain for jobs available in highly specialized occupations where, unfortunately, there is a shortage of manpower at the present time.
Mr. Speaker, this program offers tremendous potential, since we have established across the country a system for projecting occupations in Canada. We are also going to designate occupations of national importance across the country. The co-operation I referred to earlier already exists within the framework of this legislation. And as for co-operation by all parties in the House, we have tangible proof that such co-operation is possible, because we received it when this legislation was passed. All parties in the House accepted the legislation; all Canadian provinces accepted it, and just last week, the Minister of Employment and Immigration signed an agreement with the Government of Quebec, under which during the next three years, $735 million will be invested in training people in Quebec, a province that is experiencing unprecedented highs in unemployment and where technological changes have been particularly marked. We shall therefore be in a position to train large numbers of people, and especially youth, so as to be able to meet the needs of the future, to respond to technological change and to help these people become integrated in the labour market, something which is very important, especially for young people across Canada.
However, I think, Mr. Speaker, that in addition to this skill projection system and to the skill designation program which we will undertake in co-operation with the provinces, we should add a third element to that training. Now, the Skills Growth Fund is a special $108 million fund covering a two-year period which will allow us to modernize facilities to be used for occupational training. In many cases, Mr Speaker, the courses we give are unfortunately 20 years or over behind the times and do not lead to a sure or permanent job. However that Skills Growth Fund will allow us in all parts of the country, and once again in co-operation with all provincial governments, to meet immediate and future needs.
