It is obvious that this is an important change in the Occupational Training Act. Once more allow me, Mr. Speaker, to refer to my own province of Quebec where we have seen during the past year strong opposition to this so-called federal intrusion in a provincial jurisdiction. Again, our government did not see fit to refute such charges. We officials from both levels of government were allowed to negotiate and conclude an agreement. We realize after a year of negotiations what the provincial government was saying a year earlier. They signed the agreement in order to get the funds that were available to them and that were required to meet the needs of the very large Quebec labour force. This is perhaps the reason why, Mr. Speaker, I said earlier, that a new era of co-operation seems to be forthcoming in Quebec. And this is perhaps why the Quebec Minister of Manpower and Security has stated that he had just signed a treaty with the federal government. We do hope that the provincial government has indeed signed a treaty. We also hope that they will give up their political option which is out of place under the present economic circumstances and that they will truly co-operate with the federal government in trying to meet immediate needs. This can be seen in this training act and I am sure, Mr. Speaker, that in the negotiations now underway with this province in order to reach agreements about job creation, their representatives will show the same spirit of co-operation and will work in the best interests of those who elected them to the Quebec National Assembly. And, together with the federal government, they will finally succeed in creating jobs so terribly needed in the winter months. That just shows, Mr. Speaker, that the federal government has really taken the matter in hands, and that it is willing to negotiate with all available partners in an effort to find solutions.
If I may be allowed, Mr. Speaker, I would like to mention another measure announced yesterday by the federal government, to protect our Canadian workers and to make sure that most available jobs in this country will go to them. The minister announced yesterday that he was setting new immigration quotas throughout the country. Of course, these new levels do not mean that Canada will be closing its door to the world. We shall continue to accept immigrants for humanitarian reasons and adhere to the family reunion concept, both at the basis of our immigration policy. That being said, Mr. Speaker, we must nevertheless face up to the situation and realize that a large number of unemployed Canadians might otherwise have a job. That is the reason why we have lowered our immigration levels and tightened regulations concerning application for work permits in Canada. That is also why we are urging all Canadian employers who want to hire people to check first whether, somewhere in Canada, there are workers available for jobs open to all Canadians. Once again, Mr. Speaker, that is a concrete example of what our government does in the present situation to find work for as many Canadians as possible. We intend to keep this up and to maintain an open line to reach all groups, all individuals and all others who

may have constructive suggestions for finding as many jobs as possible.
If we urge all provincial and municipal governments as well as all Canadian employers to support our endeavor to find jobs, I am sure, Mr. Speaker, that at the end of this year we will realize that the funds we have set aside last week have enabled us to create 120,000 or 150,000 jobs instead of the
60,000	we had expected in the first place. We must join forces and put aside all political considerations. Now that the Quebec government has indicated-indicated, I repeat-that it is prepared to go along, it would be difficult not to expect all parties in the House and all other governments in Canada to jump on the bandwagon.
I am convinced that the initiative we took in that area last week is worthy of consideration by each and every Canadian. I am convinced as well that, once the Minister of Employment and Immigration (Mr. Axworthy) has completed his consultation process, the Canadian government will be in a position to announce a series of programs designed to contend with the current situation and to help those people who will be facing hardships this winter, thus making it a lot easier for a great many Canadians.

Mr. Speaker, I have to admit that this week we are hearing a lot about cooperation, goodwill and moderation, but earlier this year, a month or so ago, it was all confrontation and the law-nothing remotely identifiable with what the hon. member for Bonaven-ture-Iles-de-la-Madeleine (Mr. Bujold) is talking about today. So much so indeed that he would never have made that speech last year, not in that spirit, and yet the conditions then were the same. Only the blind and the incompetent could not foresee the economic conditions which were facing Canada a year ago at the time of the famous budget of the former finance minister. He was telling us that the deficit would amount to about $10 billion, that the gross national product would decline slightly, and that inflation was just about under control or, if not completely so, that its rate of increase was dropping. It was the budget of an incompetent man or of sheer dishonesty. Never before have Canadians been taken for such a ride. And the scenario was practically the same in June, except that the $10 billion deficit was revised upward to something like $19 billion. What were the economists and the Department of Finance doing? Were they not aware of the plight of our best industries in Western Canada, especially the oil industry which was being torpedoed and ransacked by this government under the National Energy Policy, and then overtaxed, as though the only milk cow in the country were the oil industry? I should like you, hon. members from Quebec and Ontario who supported your party's platform during the 1980 election campaign, and who had been outraged by our proposed 18 cents tax on a gallon of gas-only four and a half cents a litre which would barely pay for a cupful of gas now- to consider the cost of a litre of gas today and the way it is

The dear lady, I know, has always the right answer, but as far as the Canadian economy is concerned, she would not know how to get out of a turnstile. No, Mr. Speaker. I clearly recall the time the Right Hon. Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) went on TV some 14 years ago to talk to the Canadian people. What about? About ways to freeze inflation around the 6 or 7 per cent level.
"We have wrestled inflation to the ground", we heard in 1969 after the efforts announced in the late summer of 1968, as I recall. The Government have been wrestling with themselves, not with inflation. We have seen inflation go up and up as time went on. Thanks to the efforts of other Ministers and the spirit of the speech of the Hon. Member for Bonaventure-Iles-de-la-Madeleine (Mr. Bujold) which I have just heard, the purpose of the Government is to take more and more funds and spread them further and further as though the Government were hooked onto or piped into an ever growing money tree. The Hon. Minister of National Health and Welfare (Miss Begin) is a classic example, advocating programs which take money from here to spend there. Spend, spend is all the Hon. lady wants to do, not knowing, of course, that a dollar does not come out of the end of a fountain pen. That dollar must be produced by industry, but not industry which is overladen with taxes.
Hon. Members talk of the last budget exercise. Does Your Honour know that there is a hefty tax increase included in it? Of course, Hon. Members on the Government side will not tell their supporters that reducing the cap on the inflation factor in determining taxable income means a hefty tax increase. The Government will then come along and cap the indexing of inflation faced by old age pensioners and other pensioners such as public servants. They will face double taxation.
As a result of the budgetary statement of June 28, the elderly people of Canada will be hit by a double tax whammy. First of all, inflation will artificially boost their incomes so that many will be in a higher tax bracket. I do not care whether this bracket is in the lower level, the middle level or possibly in the higher level; there will be a tax increase. Then their old age pensions will be reduced or confined by the six and five formula even though we are experiencing 11 per cent inflation at the present time. Wait until Hon. Members from across the way start explaining that fact to their old age citizens! Then we will see whether their speeches are quite as laudatory of the Government's financial policies.
During the summer recess I spent five or six weeks hearing representations from industries, individuals and professional
associations on the budgetary proposals of November 12, 1981. Some of the tax provisions were thrown out of the window by the Minister of Finance (Mr. Lalonde). Others were modified. However, there will be an increase in taxes on corporations and individuals this year amounting to $1.6 billion. Next year that will rise to $2.2 billion. Those are the tax changes which were proposed by the last Finance Minister. That is a residual effect of his stay in office.
In the statement last Wednesday we heard that another $1.1 billion will be taken out of the pockets of employees and employers through an additional levy for the unemployment insurance fund. Unemployment insurance, Mr. Speaker, has to be the greatest fraud ever perpetrated on the Canadian public. There is no longer an insurance program. There is a giant welfare and transfer of revenues fund. To the extent that there is a deficit, the taxpayers of Canada must pay. Where does most of the income tax come from? Distribute that to the areas of greatest unemployment. The fund itself has been deformed from an insurance program. One should simply read the speeches of the Hon. Member for Lincoln (Mr. Mackasey) when he was Minister of Labour back in 1971, before the majority of Hon. Members opposite had even heard of the House of Commons or been elected. That former Minister, who is now a Government front bencher, merely stated that making the program universal would lay the cornerstone of a guaranteed annual income scheme for Canadians.
This was the first level, unemployment insurance. We have seen over the years how bits have been added. Actuarially, it does not make sense. There have been deficits chargeable by law to the Government of Canada because the deficit exceeds a certain figure. I had to laugh the other day when the Minister of Finance said, my goodness, isn't the Government of Canada generous to the people of Canada, the unemployed, because it is providing 60 per cent of the additional benefits that are going to be paid out of the unemployment insurance fund; all the increases shall not come out of the pockets of contributing employees and their employers. But the law says the Government of Canada must do precisely that. It has to meet the deficit and should be meeting the entire deficit. Part of it is fobbed off on employees and employers. For the rest of it we, the taxpayers of Canada, lose a little more hide and give a little more blood to the financial bloodsucker which this administration has become.
As for the Canadian economy, Mr. Speaker, I don't know how many times it has been repeated that it is now a world recession that is responsible for the problems in Canada. That is public deception. Of course, many of our markets have declined because there have been declines in other economies, but not that much. The United States, faced with the problem of inflation, has dealt with it through interest rates in order to protect the U.S. dollar. The U.S. dollar, however, under the Bretton Woods Agreement Act, is the reserve standard for the
November 2, 1982

International Monetary Fund. Therefore, what are strictly domestic requirements in the United States involving the protection of the U.S. dollar immediately become prime factors affecting world-wide economies. We have seen this all over the world, in Britain and here in Canada although whether it should have been quite so severe in Canada is open to question. I am not going to make myself an instant expert and say the Bank of Canada were right or wrong, but it is possibly a bit of both. That is a matter of judgment.
Let us look at France-and the NDP should look at France. That famous experiment in socialist thinking and socialist spending out of economic stagnation has been the biggest bust since the last Halloween balloon. There is no magical formula. But there are so many ways of damning your economy. Here in Canada the National Energy Program has affected not only the entire west, but the auto and machine industry of Ontario. An ongoing western petroleum industry requires between
30,000	and 40,000 automobiles or trucks per year, most of them coming out of Ontario. The volume of that is now reduced to 25 per cent, maybe even less.
Steel pipe? The whole bit and business has been knocked on the head by these incompetents across the way, and one might also say it was maliciously inspired, because they envied the success of the three western Provinces having petroleum and natural gas. They could not stand it. Unfortunately, the people of Ontario got hit by some degree of jealousy as well. That is not the way to build this country, by knocking down another part of it. But that is what was done.
All those famous projects in the Province of Quebec which were greeted with open arms are not going ahead. The pipelines are not going to be built. They are going to close refineries. That is what is happening. It was blind fools that went tinkering. Then what did they do? They shuffled the Minister, and lo and behold, no longer was the administration responsible. The mandarins who put together the pieces of paper, creating the schemes, which in theory should have worked, disappeared to their just rewards. So we are left with a legacy of thousands upon thousands of unemployed, including formerly highly paid people, productive people, and political unrest. One section of the country is bitterly alienated towards the rest for that reason. The Government Members strain their shoulders patting themselves on the back for the success of their policies. We will be paying $2.50 for a gallon of gasoline over a two year period. That is success?
We have then the famous organization known as FIR A, the "Herb Gray spooks". I know that other countries have screening agencies, but it takes a hearty soul armed with millions and millions of dollars to fight off the attacks on Canadians wanting to invest in the United States. The pot is not entirely black, but at least it is not formalized. In FIRA as presently constituted, it is not the Agency itself that is responsible. Every decision that has been put through the Agency is only a recommendation to a Cabinet committee presided over by the former Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce, who dillydallied and imposed his own prejudices and views on each application. When you inquired as to an application which had been filed nine months before to cover a sale that had been

agreed to and made economic sense, the Minister would not tell you anything. He would not even tell the company that was going to be bought because it was not a participant to the application. His interpretations were nothing but stupid bureaucracy. I have never seen such incompetence in my life.
That is what is chasing foreign investment. It is that image of months and months of dilly-dallying, the automatic, unofficial views that were expressed, such as: "You should change it this way; perhaps if you change it that way, we suggest you reapply but under modified terms". This sort of thing went on and on. That is why we find our friends and trading partners objecting to what is happening to foreign investment of that nature coming into Canada.
Certainly we can take a look, but do not tell us it is going to take a year. Some Provinces putting together a project of development take two years to clear all the agencies, come what may, merely to fit the ego of a lot of bureaucrats and over-swollen Government ranks. If we want to reduce public expenditure, each level of Government, including the Government of Canada, the provincial Governments and the municipal Governments should set a target of first reducing personnel by 10 per cent. I do not mean the lower paid clerks; there are far more semi-employed directors and directors-general in the Public Service of Canada. That is a ridiculous cost.
Right here in our own shop we have fatuous legislation on the books which at the present time is causing the redistribution commissions to increase the number of Members of this House by, I think, 28. We do not have a place to seat them. When one looks at what it costs per Member for staff and other facilities, one sees how silly we can be. We can stand a 10 per cent reduction of Members in this place.

That one will preserve the unexpended portion for the following year. It is always there. It is part of the atmosphere of sleight-of-hand, covering up and putting things off.
The people of Canada do not realize just how bad are the finances of the Government of Canada. Most of that is the responsibility of this administration which did not care a tinker's dam. It spent and spent and spent. A lot of it has been built up in the past ten years. The $10 of expenditure that was authorized ten years ago is now over $20 due to inflation and to Ministers bringing in programs, getting them accepted and then saying; "Where is the money? I must have the money." Instead of saying that only so much money was available for a particular program, the reverse was always the case. The net result is that the Government of Canada goes careening from ditch to ditch with wide open throttle, not knowing how much gasoline is in the tank. It does not know whether it has control of the car and hopes to blazes it will not run into somebody going the other way, because it sure does not know who is on the road.

subtopic: SUPPLEMENTARY BORROWING AUTHORITY ACT, 1982-83 (NO. 2) MEASURE TO ESTABLISH
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I welcome the opportunity to speak on the supplementary borrowing authority Bill, Bill C-128, which complements and restores Bill C-125 of July 22 last to the original borrowing amount requested at that time. A world-wide recesion has lowered the demands of other countries for Canadian products such as those drawn from our forests, mines and other industries. International oil prices, which were forecast to climb astronomically, underwent a downturn, which adversely affected our own exploration activities. Uncontrollable circumstances like these, coupled with many other similar factors, caused a weakness in our economy and a short-fall in our estimated revenues.
Simply put, the Government of Canada requires this borrowing authority to give it the financial ability to maintain all the programs that the Canadian people expect to retain as part of their own economic outlook and standard of living. I am pleased that Opposition Members have agreed to limit this debate to three days. Lengthy debate on this Bill would have been damaging to those thousand of Canadians most directly affected by the recession. To those thousands of Canadians, the economic statement recently presented by the Hon. Minister of Finance (Mr. Lalonde) has given much to hope for
in the coming months. It was a clear indication of the Government's concern for them and the situation they find themselves in as a result of the recession.
In the past few months we have been constantly pressed by the Opposition to bring in programs to help the unemployed and all of those unable to cope with the recession. Although short on solutions, they have demanded action to assist those out of work. They oppose six and five. They generally clamour for an increase in unemployment insurance benefits. They suggest expenditures be increased and taxes reduced. Some might even suggest that the Government should not be obsessed and mesmerized by the huge deficit. They say, spend more, stimulate the economy, and the next day they contradict themselves by deploring the size of the deficit, the rate of inflation, and demand the Government cut back on expenditures.
The present recession has put a tremendous strain on all governments of the western world. Accustomed to prosperity and growth, these countries must now enforce rigid economic policies in an attempt to move out of the recession.

Mr. Speaker, the level of support demanded from the Federal Government during a recession is considerable. No one can escape the present economic situation. Some will be even more at risk because of their particular situation. The Government will have to meet the requirements of those who are most affected by the recession. Canada has one of the best social systems in the world, whether it be our Unemployment Insurance Plan, our social welfare programs or our income security measures. This system was designed to protect Canadians during a recession as well as in more prosperous times. Our Government, and the Liberal Party in fact, has always given the priority in its ideology to our social institutions. The recent statement of the Minister of Finance (Mr. Lalonde) reassured Canadians that the Government will protect them throughout the recession. The Unemployment Insurance Plan will remain intact. Moreover, the Government will respond to the appeals of thousands of Canadians now deprived of job opportunities. Maintaining a comprehensive Unemployment Insurance Plan and very generous social programs is a very difficult task, especially when the Government is committed to apply strict fiscal policies. When the Government itself must tighten its belt and keep the deficit at a reasonable level, how is it possible to maintain our Unemployment Insurance Plan and social programs? How can we create jobs for the victims of the recession and give support to the private sector without increasing the deficit even more? That is the dilemma now facing all Western countries. Some of them have chosen to cut their spending for social security programs. Canada has chosen differently. We have been able to find a solution which will not jeopardize those who are hardest hit by the recession. We shall also limit our spending so as to reduce the potential inflationary impact of the deficit on the national economy. This will be done on the basis of an equitable formula without our having to weaken our social institutions. The bill now under consideration is an integral
November 2, 1982

part of the economic and social formula which will put us back on the road to prosperity.

I would like to review our economic policy with a view to the West, Mr. Speaker. The federal Government is committed to securing Canadians' economic future, and to do so involves addressing the challenges and pursuing the opportunities for economic development which present themselves in the various regions of this country. I intend to focus on the opportunities and constraints facing the western provinces and comment on the federal Government's response to these.
A year ago, in November, 1981, the federal Government issued a major policy document entitled "Economic Development for Canada in the 1980s". That document discussed the challenges and strategic opportunities for the national and regional economies, and went on to outline the Government's policies and priorities for national economic development. While it was clearly stated that there were distinct problems and development issues to be addressed in every region, it was also pointed out that unique opportunities for economic growth and development could be identified in every region.
Since that policy document was issued, and even prior to that, the Government has taken action to identify and overcome the constraints to economic development which prevail in the western provinces, and aggressively to pursue those opportunities which exist in the west for economic growth in this decade and beyond. Last Wednesday, in the statement on the economic outlook by the Hon. Minister of Finance, the federal Government reconfirmed its commitment to economic development and renewal across Canada.
Aside from issuing the earlier mentioned document on economic development, this Government introduced a number of measures which, while general in application, would have some impact on the economy of the western provinces. For example, the special farm financial assistance program was reintroduced in an expanded form. This program, which was designed for those farmers who would be unable to stay in business if they had to borrow at the going interest rate, provided subsidized Farm Credit Corporation loans to farmers in distress. A fund of $50 million was set aside for this program.
In the June 28 budget the Government announced a number of new housing measures designed to create new jobs in the construction industry, to improve access to home ownership, to assist those facing mortgage renewal difficulties and to ensure the availability of rental accommodation. An intensive program for the construction of new rental units was introduced to provide an interest free loan of $7,500 or more per rental unit for 30,000 units allocated to tight market areas across the country. I am pleased to add the Minister's announcement on Wednesday to the effect that the $3,000 home ownership stimulation grant will be extended to the end of April, 1983 for new houses. This announcement was certainly welcomed by the western construction industry.
Supplementary Borrowing Authority
In order to direct federal policies and programs to the strategic opportunities for Canadian economic development, the Government identified five priority areas, namely, industrial development, resource development, transportation capacity, export promotion, and human resources. Under each of these headings objectives were identified and examples of initiatives under way or proposed were given. In many instances the western Provinces figures prominently as major contributors to Canada's economic future or as recipients of federal aid.
In terms of developing industry, the Government is committed to developing policies and programs to ensure, among other things, that innovation becomes a major factor in enhancing the competitiveness and productivity of Canadian industry.
The Government has committed itself to a major increase in the level of research and development activity in Canada and has established research and development targets for the public and private sectors. At the end of 1981 the federal Government had met, and indeed exceeded, the R and D expenditure target it had set for itself. More recent federal initiatives in this area of activity include new funding for the establishment of micro-electronic centres in Vancouver, Edmonton and Winnipeg.
In terms of developing natural resources, the federal Government agreed to undertake new initiatives in key resource based sectors, and the western Provinces, with their vast wealth of resources, will figure prominently in any policies and programs implemented in these areas.
The federal Government undertook to continue consultation with the Provinces concerning measures to enhance the longer-term performance of the forest-based industries and to continue to play a strong role in encouraging research and development in the mining industry.
I want to digress from the economic strategy in the eighties for a moment to reflect on a side issue, Mr. Speaker. We hear people say, with a great deal of hindsight, that the Canadian Government underestimated the severity of the current recession and did not adopt timely measures to turn it around.
In the area of rail transportation, we must recognize the fact that our railway system was not overburdened this year. Record grain movements were established, partly because our other commodities did not compete as strongly with grain movements as in prior years for cars, for track time on rail lines, for engines and for railway crews, at the same time that grain was being transported to ports.
Canadians do not want to rely on hindsight when our economy takes a turn for the better. We must be prepared to seize our opportunities. For this reason, I am sure that all parties are in agreement and acknowledge that the leading opportunity for Canadian economic renewal lies in the development of Canada's rich bounty of natural resources. However, capturing the benefits of a resource-based expansion will place heavy demands on the transportation system. Unless major investments are made in the near future, the capacity

November 2, 1982
Supplementary Borrowing Authority
constraints in the western transportation system will be evident by the mid-eighties.
Under economic development in the eighties, transportation was identified as a development priority. On February 8, 1982 the Minister of Transport (Mr. Pepin) announced the Government of Canada's policy on western rail transportation. The statement recognized that the western Canadian economy is rapidly growing and diversifying, and will continue to do so throughout the 1980s. The resource sector is the source of much of this western growth, and western resources have been and will continue to be moved predominantly by rail. Consequently, the Government decided that a major initiative was required if the economic expansion under way was to continue, and that a comprehensive approach should be implemented to ensure that the west had adequate rail capacity.
The Minister of Transport appointed Dr. Clay Gilson of the University of Manitoba as the federal representative on western grain transportation, to lead discussions with western farm organizations and the railways on how the Government's policy statement should be translated into specific measures. After months of consultations with representatives of nine major western farm organizations and the two national railways, Dr. Gilson submitted his report on consultations and recommendations regarding western grain transportation to the Minister of Transport.
In August, the Minister announced that the Government would establish special task forces to continue and conclude work on the recommendations contained in the Gilson Report on western grain transportation.
Mr. Pepin also tabled in Parliament a Government policy response stating that the Government had decided to accept in principle the main thrust of the Gilson Report now, subject to later decisions about the financial considerations and the reports of the task forces concerning the implementation aspects of a central co-ordinating agency for grain transportation, a new freight rate structure and new legislation for grain transportation.
In addressing the issue of assuring the nation that the west had adequate rail capacity, the Government stressed the major potential benefits of this initiative for western Canada and the country as a whole, including large-scale railway investments, improvements in the grain transportation system, increased resource development and economic diversification.
To help achieve these benefits, the Government committed itself to contributing some $3.2 billion over the four-year period of 1982-83 through 1985-86 for western transportation needs and to the introduction of new transportation legislation. Such a statutory framework would incorporate a commitment by the Government to pay the Crow benefit in perpetuity and to demand performance and service guarantees from the railways in return for adequate compensation for current grain transportation losses.
Railway investments amounting to some $11.8 billion, in 1982 dollars, are planned over the decade to 1991 and will generate substantial economic activity, not only in the west but
in virtually every region of the country. In addition to major construction activity and sourcing of materials in the western provinces, the railways' requirements for steel rail, locomotives, rolling stock and electronic equipment will provide a major stimulus over the period, to the manufacturing sector, in all of Canada.
This brings us to the very recent announcement made by the Minister of Finance. As the Minister pointed out, the Government is earmarking up to $400 million more to provide some additional flexibility toward the satisfactory Crow rate resolution and to provide for initiatives such as the extension of special capital cost allowances which, if satisfactory arrangements can be made with the Minister of Transport, would speed up expansion and modernization of western rail capacity. As the Minister noted, the Government is determined to meet the challenge of railway capacity with its comprehensive approach to expand the western rail transportation system and to modernize the freight rate regime for grain.
Early action will ensure that railways will be in a position to increase rail capacity, as required, to move the substantially higher volumes of export commodities projected from the middle of the decade onward. Expansion of western rail capacity is critical to Canada's economic development in the 1980s. It will pave the way for marketing of additional coal, potash and sulphur resources as well as increased exports of grain. The over-all plan will also stimulate western agricultural development and facilitate economic diversification. As a result of direct railway and Government expenditures, it is estimated that some 400,000 person-years of employment will ultimately be generated across the country.
In addition to the commitment to expand the western rail transportation system and modernize the freight rate regime for grain, the federal Government has undertaken other initiatives in the transportation field which will help us promote our exports. The Government has committed $27 million to develop the infrastructure for a new grain terminal at Prince Rupert and another $4 million for the road access to it. To improve Canada's capacity to ship coal, particularly to new Pacific Rim markets, the capacity of the Roberts Bank terminal at Vancouver will be quadrupled, and new harbour and rail facilities will be constructed at Prince Rupert in connection with northeast British Columbia coal deposits. Legislation was recently passed providing for greater autonomy at the local level for National Harbours Board ports.
Returning to the development priorities and specifically the need to develop human resources, the Government is taking measures to identify the manpower needs of various industrial sectors and to direct strategies to match skills with these needs. Particular attention is being given to disadvantaged Canadians and, as was mentioned earlier, $345 million has been allocated in the period 1985-86 to support new economic development initiatives directed toward increased job opportunities for native peoples.
November 2, 1982

The federal Government's contribution to the economic development of western provinces arises not only from new programs and initiatives but also from existing and ongoing programs. For example, DREE expenditures during 1980-81 in the western region, including Yukon and the Northwest Territories, exceeded $200 million. Of this sum, approximately $72.6 million was for subsidiary agreements, $20.5 million for industrial incentives, $82.3 million for Prairie Farm Rehabilitation Administration Programs, and the remainder for activities such as special ARDA agreements under the Agricultural and Rural Development Act. Special ARDA agreements involve special programs to ensure that rural residents, particularly those of native descent, are able to benefit from rural development programs in terms of increased employment and income and better living conditions. Such agreements exist with Manitoba, Saskatchewan, British Columbia, the Northwest Territories and Yukon. They are administered in each area by a committee comprised of representatives of the provincial or territorial Government, the federal Government and native residents of the communities involved.
They also support the Prairie Farm Rehabilitation Administration Program which was started years ago in drought areas to ensure that municipalities and other areas would have sufficient water supply. This Program is active, and there are agreements with the Province of Manitoba and other Provinces to make sure that they have adequate water facilities to supply the needs of their citizens.
Earlier this year the federal Government implemented a major policy and administrative reorganization, the main thrust of which was to provide a government-wide focus on regional development. A Cabinet Committee on Economic and Regional Development was established, as well as a new Ministry of State for Economic and Regional Development, the new Department of Regional Industrial Expansion and the regional fund to be used for special regional economic development initiatives. Federal economic development co-ordinators, the most senior economic development officials in each of the regions, have been named for all the Provinces, and work is under way to devise over-all economic strategies for each of the Provinces. Clearly, while the actors involved in regional development may change somewhat and certain aid delivery vehicles may be identified by a different name, the federal Government has reaffirmed, if not expanded upon, its commitment to balanced regional development.
As a final point it is worth noting that the Canadian Grain Commission recently reduced their proposed increases in maximum tariffs of 8 per cent to 10 per cent or higher, as well as the fees charged for services to the grain industry, to conform with the 6 per cent restraint policy for this year. Harnessing the resources of the Canadian economy is a national enterprise which includes but extends beyond the interests of particular regions or sectors. The Government of Canada must and has assumed a leadership role in the field of economic development, as evidenced by the recent transportation initiatives in the west and other activities across the
Supplementary Borrowing Authority
country. However, it has done so bearing in mind and being sensitive to the local context in which each Canadian works, lives and invests. This borrowing authority Bill is an integral part of the economic proposals that will set us off on the road to recovery. I urge all Members of the House to support Bill C-128.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I want to take just a few moments this evening to contribute to this semi budget debate we are having. The point has been made that the economic statement delivered by the new Minister of Finance (Mr. Lalonde) last Wednesday was much closer to a budget than many of the budgets we have had. Although I am not sure that is completely accurate. In a lot of ways it resembled an "unbudget" because most of the important statements in the document were undoing the provisions of the November 12, 1981 budget, which slowly and surely over the course of a year has been totally undone.
The Bill we are discussing is the borrowing authority Bill to give the Governor in Council the authority to borrow another $4 billion. That is an astronomical amount of money, except in comparison to this year's deficit, which is $23.6 billion. What an unbelievable state of affairs. We are asking future taxpayers to pay for one-third of our expenditures today, piling on top of existing debt another $23.6 billion in a deficit this year on a public accounts basis. I said a public accounts basis because on a national accounts basis, that is on a more accurate basis, the deficit is a lot higher than $23.6 billion. The picture is in fact a whole lot worse than the incredibly bad picture which the Minister of Finance gave us last Wednesday. This $23.6 billion is not the total deficit because the Government engages in book cooking, the kind of book cooking that would get a private company or an individual engaged in the same kind of exercise in trouble.
Is that a statement made by a partisan Member of the Opposition using hyperbole, Mr. Speaker? I would refer Hon. Members of the House to the Auditor General's Report. The public accounts were tabled last Friday. Carried in the public

November 2, 1982
Supplementary Borrowing Authority
accounts of Canada, the accounts of the Government of Canada, is $16 billion in non-existing assets. In other words, there is $16 billion of spending on assets which the Auditor General says do not exist. If a company did that, it would be delisted from the stock exchange. The executives and directors of such a company would be in great trouble with regulatory authorities. Lawsuits may be launched. There could be all manner of retribution levied against an organization that would have the audacity, the gall or the fraudulent intent to put forward accounts so obviously in error. Yet here we have the Government of Canada, our government, putting out a set of books which the Auditor General says are in error by $ 16 billion. The Government gets away with this because the amount of money is so colossal that no one can get his mind around it. It is almost beyond comprehension. It is as Adolf Hitler knew so well, that if the distortion is big enough, it just escapes people. There is no way they can handle it. That is what we have from this Government.
Not included in the horrendous deficit figure is Crown Corporation borrowing. Crown Corporations are, in the jargon, "Agents of Her Majesty", which means nothing more than that the debts of a Crown Corporation are the same as the direct debts of the Government. Whether it is the Minister of Finance who borrows money from the Government of Canada or Jack Horner who borrows on behalf of the CNR, the effect is the same. You and I are responsible for paying back the borrowings.
The borrowings of the Minister of Finance show up in the public accounts. Jack Horner's borrowings do not, nor do the borrowings of Bill Hopper or Nick Ebiger, nor do the borrowings of any one of these other people in this parallel civil service operating out there on their own who are indebting you and me and future generations.
None of the deficits being run up in these organizations, none of the borrowing, none of the spending show up in the accounts of Canada. Yet, in terms of their impact, they are every bit the same as if they were spent directly by the Government. That is why when the Minister lays out projections for spending and revenues this year, it is only a fool who takes what he lays before us at face value. They are most certainly not an accurate portrayal of what is happening.
I want to deal with one particular debt of a Crown Corporation of which we have become aware recently, interestingly enough on Saturday afternoon. Clearly it is amazing to observe this Government in operation and to see the gall and hypocrisy with which it operates. I believe it was Thursday evening when Senator Keith Davey was lecturing from a podium about how terrible the media in this country is. He said that the Government cannot trust the media to carry its message and that the media cannot be trusted. Two days later, we saw the most blatant example of how the Government manipulates news, manipulates the media and manipulates public opinion. When is the time to make an embarrassing announcement, Mr. Speaker? It is on Saturday afternoon when you know that most people have the weekend off and very few journalists are working. Is it not interesting that on the "Sunday Morning" CBC program Bill Hopper was
answering a bunch of creampuff questions from a CBC reporter. That program was in the can on Friday but, somehow, the announcement did not come out until Saturday. Yet there was Bill Hopper with all the perfect answers to the creampuff questions being put to him. There was not one single, reasonable or appropriate question asked by that reporter.
That shows skill, Mr. Speaker, and I admit that Bill Hopper is an amazingly effective politician, news manager, manipulator of public opinion. While he is not an oil man, he is all these other things, and very good at it. I have the bruises to prove it. But for goodness' sakes, do not insult my intelligence and the intelligence of all Canadians by turning Senator Keith Davey loose to say, "It is terrible that we cannot trust the media to take our fair and reasonable message around the country". What hypocricy!
On Saturday we were told that Petro-Canada was going to buy the downstream assets of BP Canada for $347.5 million. That is a colossal amount of money, given that not one job will be created out of that purchase or one barrel of oil added. Now we find out that that statement about the $347.5 million was false. In fact, the total purchase cost is closer to $600 million, as we discovered in today's Globe and Mail. Long after it is settled in everyone's mind that the purchase price is $350 million-that is the figure publicized and which is contained in most files-we find that the real figure is $600 million because, in addition to the $347.5 million for the steel and real estate, there is $180 million for inventory and a $70 million debt that Petro-Canada is picking up for BP. Therefore, the figure is $600 million and not $347 million. I offer you again one further example for the observation of the Auditor General that you cannot trust the Government because it lies about its figures. It is further evidence of why anyone who takes what is said by that group of people and their underlings at face value is a fool to accept it. It seldom bears any resemblance to the truth.
Petro-Canada is spending $600 million, and the Minister, Bill Hopper and Joel Bell say that it will not cost the taxpayers a cent. But the advertisement says, that Petro-Canada is ours. Therefore, if its assets are our assets, its debts are our debts. That $600 million is our debt in the same manner as the Minister of Finance's debts are our debts.
That $600 million is being spent to purchase existing, inplace assets without a single new job being created. In fact, jobs will be lost because throughout Quebec and parts of Ontario, Fina-which is now Petro-Canada-and BP were frequently competitors on the same corner. BP and Petro-Canada are next door neighbours in my neighbourhood in Ottawa. While there were previously two marketing departments, there will now be one marketing department because one of those service stations will close down. As a result, there will be fewer jobs if Petro-Canada rationalizes its employees.
The Government is spending $600 million of our money, decreasing the number of jobs and not gaining one extra piece
November 2, 1982

of hardware, real estate, barrell of oil or anything else for Canada. Of course, that $600 million does not form part of the $23.6 billion deficit. It is not included in the Government's figures. It is not covered by this borrowing authority Bill because, in this perverse system which we have, the Minister of Finance is required to have borrowing authority while Bill Hopper does not. This Parliament has the right to vote on the authority of the Minister of Finance to borrow money. Bill Hopper, Jack Horner and the other 400 Crown corporation presidents and chairmen can borrow what they desire. Canadians are obliged to pay it, but as the elected representatives of the people we do not have the right to say yea or nay. That is parliamentary democracy for you. It the Government has $600 million to spend, why did it not reduce the unemployment insurance premium entries? There is a $1.7 billion increase in premiums which will cost perhaps 60,000 jobs because it is making it more difficult for small and new businesses to hire new employees. Why did the Government not reduce that expenditure if it has $600 million to spend?
Why not reduce the taxes on gasoline and make a half baked attempt to honour the election promises that were made by the Liberal Party, those promises of "Vote Liberal and you will not have to pa^ high prices for gasoline." Do you remember those advertisements, Mr. Speaker? If the Government now has $600 million extra, why does it not reduce the taxes on gasoline and make a half hearted attempt to honour that election promise?
Why not spend the money on job creation if the Government does have $600 million to spend? Why does the Government not try something new and just not spend it?
If some of the geniuses who advise that pack over there feel that it is appropriate for Petro-Canada to spend another $600 million, let me suggest a way in which Petro-Canada could spend that money and, in fact, contribute something to Canada in the process. First, let us suppose that the Minister of Finance was correct when he said, in answer to questions I raised yesterday, that Petro-Canada was not going to borrow money in Canada but was going to borrow it offshore, even though Joel Bell, Vice-President of Finance, said they had not made that decision as yet. However, let us assume that the Minister of Finance was right and Petro-Canada will borrow the money offshore. Now, let us suppose that Petro-Canada took that $600 million and invested it in exploration for new oil in Canada. The rough industry average indicates that for every $50,000 of expenditure, one can expect oil production of a barrel of oil per day. Assuming that Petro-Canada is as good as the average oil company-which is a major concession because I do not believe that fact and the figures do not back it up-this means that Petro-Canada would be able to produce
12,000	barrels of oil per day from that expenditure of $600 million for exploration. We would produce 12,000 barrels of oil per day in Canada and eliminate the need to import that oil from Mexico, Saudi Arabia and Venezuela. That would save us $220 million a year in foreign exchange. In other words, in two years and nine months we would be able to pay off the foreign source from which we borrowed the $600 million. We
Supplementary Borrowing Authority
would still have 12,000 barrels of oil in production and maintain the income of $220 million a year for the benefit of
Canada.
A rough rule of thumb in regard to capital expenditures is that for every $50,000 of capital expenditure there is a new job created. If the government spent that $600 million in Canada on capital expenditures, namely exploration and development, it would generate 12,000 jobs. Half of all the money spent in this country-that is, the gross national product-ends up in the Government coffers as taxes of one sort or another. Half of that amount goes to the federal Government and the other half goes to the Provinces and municipal Governments. Therefore, the total government revenue from that $600 million would be $300 million. The federal Government would receive $150 million. In addition, those 12,000 people would not be collecting unemployment insurance. There would be a saving of $120 million.
Let us consider this in summary. If, instead of buying an existing refinery and a bunch of existing service stations and contributing nothing new, in fact costing jobs to Canada, Petro-Canada had used that money for oil exploration here in Canada, the federal Government would receive $150 million in extra revenue. There would be a reduced call on unemployment insurance premiums of $120 million, meaning that the net expenditures of the Government and therefore the deficit would be reduced by $270 million, and provincial and municipal Governments would receive another $150 million. There would be a decrease in our current account deficit with the rest of the world of $220 million a year in today's dollars, with a resulting reduction of pressure on interest rates and the value of the dollar. There would be 12,000 Canadians employed rather than unemployed as the case is now. Therefore, instead of $600 million spent, with no benefit whatsoever to Canada, the Government could have spent it that way with some benefit to Canada.
What have we gained from this purchase, this increased indebtedness of $600 million? Will it help to create jobs? No. Will it help to fight inflation? No. Will it help old age pensioners? No. Will it help miners, forestry workers, fishermen or farmers? No, no, no and no. Why, then? Has the private sector failed us? Does the private sector not know how to peddle gasoline? Does anyone in this country have difficulty buying gasoline from a private operator? Is the private sector in this country so terrible in that it does not know how to run service stations that Big Brother must get into the business of running service stations and filling up our tanks? Is that why? Why, for goodness' sake, is the Government of Canada, with all its responsibilities and with all the problems facing this country, in the business of peddling gasoline? It makes one wonder. If the Government is interested in the Canagrex Bill, one can surely predict that it will soon be running McDonald's hamburger stands, because if it makes sense for Petro-Canada to pump gas, it makes sense for Canagrex to sell hamburgers.

speechtext:
Why, then, is Petro-Canada buying out these service stations? Why is the Government of Canada in the business of peddling gasoline? The reasons are twofold. The first one relates to political propaganda. The reason is the same reason that Goodyear has blimps. There are some Petro-Canada signs around with the Maple Leaf on them, and Goodyear has blimps with "Goodyear" printed on them. It is pure and simple propaganda the Government has in mind. Certainly, it will not result in cheaper gasoline. It is more expensive gasoline. We must pay for the Government's extravagances. However, the related reason is that it is very good for the employees of Petro-Canada. Petro-Canada has become a very large corporation. Its chief executive officer should have his own jet, should he not? Of course, big corporations have private jets. Bill Hopper has a nice new Canadair Challenger. It is so fast that he did not even have to move his family to Calgary. His officer is there, but he lives here. What the heck! He can come home to supper in one of these Canadair jets. It only costs $5,000 or $10,000 an hour to operate. That is peanuts to a high roller like Bill Hopper. He has his own executive jet. He is just having himself a whale of a time. The Marketing Vice-President of Petro-Canada now has, 1,600 more stations to run. What a thrill when he comes into his office in the morning and looks at a map with little pins all over it. He says, "Those are all mine. I run those. Those guys are all mine. I run them all". It is a real thrill for the employees of Petro-Canada. They are having a ball at our expense.
There is a second reason which is that the decision was made as a result of faulty business judgment. The refining and marketing of gasoline has been profitable for two out of the last 20 years. Those two years were 1978 and 1979. In 1978 Petro-Canada went out and bought an oil company, Pacific Petroleum, which happened to own a refinery and some service stations. Petro-Canada bought it at exactly the time when refining and marketing was profitable. Bill Hopper thought he had found the money pump, the money tree. He could not believe it! The refinery and service stations were as lucrative as all getout. The money was rolling in. He said, "Holy moly, have I got a way to finance my Canadair jet and the rest of my growth in the future." That is why Petro-Canada bought Fina. It thought it had found the money pump. It opened up the Fina station, cleaned it up, paved it, polished it up, put on new plastic and new signs. People came in to buy gas and Petro-Canada said, "We really have it. We could sell as much gas as we want. All we have to do is put up stations, put on signs with the Maple Leaf, and business rolls in".
The problem is that there is something in marketing called the "new station phenomenon". As one is driving down the street, suddenly before one's eyes there appears a brand new station with new fresh asphalt, the pumps are new and shining, the windows are clear and it looks nice, not like a dirty old service station, so one drives in. There is a tendency to do that. It does not make any difference how one's car operates, but somehow everything looks nice. However, in a month or two the station starts to get as dirty as the station of the guy a little
closer to home, so one stops there and goes back to one's old patterns, and that little blip in sales is just that, a blip in sales.
That is precisely what is happening to Petro-Canada in western Canada. It is being blamed, of course, on anti-Ottawa feelings out there and so forth. But in fact it is just that the stations out there are no longer new. That is all. When they were new, traffic came in. They are no longer new. Some of the Fina stations are now running into the same problem. So what we have here is an executive of a company who may believe, at least partially, that this was a good business decision. In fact, it was a lousy business decision because refining and marketing do not make money. Oh, they will get market shares initially. Oh, yes, when Petro-Canada spends $10,000 or $20,000 to renovate each station, that, by the way, is in addition to the $600 million 1 have discussed. When some tens of millions of dollars are spent to renovate all the stations, there will be a little blip in traffic, but it will not be enough to make the money to pay the interest on the loan. We, the taxpayers, will have to come up with more money again to keep that operation going.
1 have listened to some Hon. Members opposite defending this $4 billion in extra borrowing authority. In essence, they have been standing up and saying to the people of Canada, "Trust us, we have your futures in mind; we are doing good things. As trustees of your money, we are doing a good job". Only a fool would believe any of that tripe. Ed Clarke certainly does not believe it on his $200,000 sabbatical in Paris. Certainly, no one who knows anything about this Petro-Canada purchase will believe it. How can we end Canada's disastrous economic performance when we are twenty-third in productivity out of 23 OECD nations and when our standard of living is fourteenth as opposed to second as it was two years ago? We are going to end all that if, and only if, we return to honesty, decency and a modicum of intelligence about how we spend the taxpayers' money. If the new Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Mr. Chretien) had simply done some back-of-the-envelope calculations, he would have quickly realized that another $600 million just to change the logo on some gas pumps is not a good expenditure for Canada. If that money is available, spending it on exploration would employ
12,000	Canadians, would generate $270 million for the Treasury, and would provide Canadians with 12,000 barrels of oil a day which they would not have to import from other parts of the world. You do not have to be a genius to figure that out, Mr. Speaker, Apparently, no one over there has thought beyond how nice it would be to have a Maple Leaf service station in every constituency in the country, so it costs the taxpayer a few hundred million dollars. Who can understand those figures? Who knows how much $24 billion is? It is quite beyond the capabilities of anyone to grasp the significance of it, and because of that failing of the human mind, we keep getting ripped off by that crew over there. I hope soon, Mr. Speaker, those who sit over there who have a modicum of shame, or sense of responsibility, will recognize what is happening and join the rest of us to put an end to it.
November 2, 1982

Thank you, Mr. Speaker. Tonight I speak for my Party on Bill C-128 which is a Bill to borrow $4 billion. I remember when I was about six years old. It was in 1937, in the wintertime. That was the worst year of the Depression in Saskatchewan. One day my father and a neighbor drove in sleighs with teams of horses to a village about 15 miles away to get some relief straw. The straw was to be used to feed starving cattle. Neither my father nor the neighbor had a single nickel, dime or quarter to rub against each other, not a single coin. They had made this trip several times.
On the neighbor's farm they made their own butter, and each time the neighbor would take a pound of homemade butter with him when he went to the village and he would trade it to the man who ran the restaurant for two cups of coffee, worth five cents each. He would take lunch with him and would go to the little restaurant after loading the straw, eat his lunch, drink his coffee and go home. On that particular day he started off for the village in a blizzard. Taking the pound of butter, he went to the restaurant and asked for the trade. The man who ran the restaurant said the butter is only worth five cents today. The neighbor walked to the door and threw it out into the blizzard because he could not buy two cups of coffee. My father told me that story many times, and I remember the day it happened.
My father had one great fear in his life which could be expressed in a four-letter word, debt. He is dead now, God rest him, but if he knew that tonight I was speaking about a Bill that will put our country $4 billion more into debt, he would simply roll over in his grave, glad that he died.
I tell that story, because, to begin with, I do believe that we have come to a different time in history. I believe that the way to handle social and economic problems that was possible 20, 30, 40 years ago, even ten years ago, is not possible any more. Every one of the Hon. Members in this House of Commons has knocked on a lot of doors. That is part and parcel of what politicians have to do. I knocked on a lot of doors this summer in my constituency and also in other parts of Canada for other people as well. This is always a new experience because behind each door there is another person, another family, another story. I personally like to knock on doors, meet people and hear what they have to say, even when many times they tell me about most serious problems. This summer, though, I found there was a different response because people in Canada, not only in my constituency, have great difficulty in understanding what is going on. It is impossible to explain to a person who is out of work, or a family unit that has broken down because unemployment has become a new stress. It goes beyond the ordinary stresses with which a family can cope. The stress of unemployment is such that it comes as the last straw.
Many people address the question to me that I would like to speak about tonight. The question is: "What are you people doing in Parliament? Do you not realize how serious the problem is? We see you people on television calling each other names, standing up and shouting. You make a point or you do not, but what is that doing to help our problem?" I can explain
Supplementary Borrowing Authority
that the House of Commons is an old tradition which is set up with two sides far enough apart so they cannot hit each other with a sword. These things can be explained, but that does not say very much to a person who is unemployed or whose marriage is under some kind of stress, or a pensioner who is afraid his pension will be cut back, because those people have lost faith in those they believed were able to solve their problems.
I would like to speak a little about the credibility or believa-bility of myself and every other Member in this House of Commons. Since I came to Ottawa about three years ago 1 have not met anyone here who is not serious. I cannot honestly say I have met anyone in any of the three parties who is not serious. Anyone who gets elected to the House of Commons has to be serious. Why is it that once we get here we lose credibility? I would like to share my ideas as to what I think is happening. Credibility is very close to what we understand as the truth. For me, however, I would like to say, there is truth around me, in this room, in the people here, in the things I would like to know, the things that I can learn. I can learn this truth and it becomes part of me, is me, in the sense I can get that truth from my experience. The best way to get it is from a good teacher. I believe that political people have the responsibility to be good teachers. Political people have to understand the truth and, as far as possible, express that truth so that it becomes part and parcel of another person so that they understand the truth. The responsibility of understanding the truth today is a grave responsibility. It is not an easy responsibility. It is a difficult responsibility because the truth is so complicated.
On top of that, however, the truth has to be expressed in such a way that the other people will have no difficulty in believing it, because the person who gives the truth and who speaks the truth, whatever that happens to be, is credible so there is the reality of the truth and the reality of the credibility that I or whoever else is speaking must have.
I understand a teacher to be a person who is able somehow or other to clean off my mind or my intellect in such a way that I can see what is out there. An old teacher that I had when I was studying in the seminary, using an old scholastic idea, talked about the reality of the truth around me. It was as if there were a dirty window between me and the truth. A good teacher is able to clean the window in such a way that I suddenly see what is right, what is true.
Several weeks ago the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau), in a series of talks over television, indicated to the country what he understood and believed to be the truth. I have no reason to doubt that he was attempting to explain to us what he believed to be the truth. I would have to say in all honesty that I felt some of the points the Prime Minister was making were just as I saw them.
He spoke about the fact that Canada really has to be part and parcel of the modern world, that Canada can no longer

expect to have a special status just because it is Canada, that in the world of competition today we cannot expect to have preference just simply because you are Canada. That is the truth. However, as I visited and knocked on the doors of people, they did not believe it. The Prime Minister was not credible.
At a time like that, and this is my suggestion only, a person who has that kind of grave responsibility has to really think seriously about his or her future. In that very serious role as a national leader, if a person has lost credibility, what does he do? That is something the Prime Minister will have to think about seriously, because most Canadians feel he has lost credibility. That is too bad because when a person has lost credibility and is still speaking the reality or the truth, everybody suffers. They will finally say, "That is not true because you said it". It gets to the point where a person is, as I and everybody here is, being tested on his credibility all the time. That is the same as saying two and two are four and the person hearing it says it is not true. Why is it not true? "Because you said it". That is an extremely serious thing at this time in history.
I believe there is another way that truth comes. It is the way that truth has come in the tradition of the Judaic Christian background of which I come. It is the truth that comes through the voice of prophets. This is the more difficult kind of truth.
There are definitely fewer prophets than there are teachers. At a time like this, it is important to look at people around the world, here or wherever, who somehow are indicating to us truths. I am going to speak later about what I believe to be an extremely important truth that is never mentioned in the economic debates that we have in this House, the truth that one of the equations that is missing is the build-up of arms around the world and the taking away from people of the world the basic things to keep them alive. I will fill out that point as I go along.
A prophet is a person who is able to say the truth as it exists now. A prophet is one who is able, in the history of our Judaic Christian background, to speak the truth now. He is a very difficult person to have around because people know that is the truth and do not want to accept it.
There are certain qualities about the prophet, at least in the Judaic Christian religion, that make him or her special. The quality that is most important is for the prophet to be a person who is not seeking power. A prophet is a person who is on the side of the poor. A prophet is a person who, very probably, himself lives poorly.
There have been prophets in the political world. Sometimes different groups are more prone to think that they are prophets than others. I would say that in general my colleagues have a little bit of that problem at times, but it is proper to criticize ourselves in that respect because we do have within our Party that tradition.
I believe the founder of this Party, J. S. Woodsworth, was looked upon by the people in this Parliament as a prophet. I like to think that today, because he is here with us, the Hon.
Member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) has been respected in these chambers and across the land as a person who is in that category. He obviously did not come here to be powerful but came here to speak the truth about the situation that affected the poor.
I believe this House respects him. I think people looked upon the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre as a person who was speaking the truth with no intention of gaining power for himself. That is an important distinction that we have to be aware of today as I continue in my remarks.
Truth as it relates to people around us can come to us from our experience, from a good teacher or through the person who is a prophet.
I believe we are in times that are very different. I believe that right today Canada is in a world situation that has never really existed before. It is important that we all look at some of the factors that are bringing it about. Through the course of history there have been different sectors of society that have had a special powerful voice. I would say that sometimes it was the kings. The kings were the ones who spoke, and everybody said that is the truth. At other times I would say there were ecclesiastical societies. The priests or bishops would speak, and everybody would say that is the truth. During the last 25, 30 or 50 years the scientists would say certain things, and everybody would say that is the truth.
As we went through each of those different levels or sectors of history, it was difficult to see that all those groups had the truth. Today, however, I think the people who seem to be trying to tell us that they have the truth are basically the economists, yet we get so much different input, different facts and different stories from the group which call themselves economists. I realize that the science of economics is a very complicated science. I realize that if one looks at all the forces which go to make up the science of economics, no matter where it happens to be or who it happens to affect, it is a very complicated subject. To me the science of economics is not unlike the science of meteorology, the science of the weather. How does a person forecast the weather? Well, once in a while the weather person is able to take all the different components that make up weather such as wind, heat, ocean currents and others, and put them together in such a way that they can say that tomorrow it will be sunny with a chance of showers, or something like that. Quite often they are right. Then again, sometimes they are wrong. Economics, on the other hand, has to do with markets, production, interest rates, all these different forces which come together into what we call the economic situation at a given moment. One person will say interest rates go up because we have to stop inflation. It is interesting that I am talking on the very day that the Congressional elections are being held in the U.S. Interest rates go up when a President is elected in the United States, a President who is surrounded by millionnaire advisers, because it has never been a better time to be a millionnaire in the U.S. than in the last two years, and interest rates go down prior to an election. We have watched that happen just in the last two months.

In any event, when it comes to the whole question of the current economic picture, I believe there are two huge hurricanes which have not been taken account of in putting together this economic package. If I could go back to the notion of how weather is predicted and how economics are predicted, there are, as I said, two huge hurricane-type storms taking place within our particular economic weather picture, and they are not being taken seriously by most of the economists who are telling us which way to go. One of those storms is the linkage we now have with the developing world, a group of countries that not so very long ago were powerless to compete with North America, Europe and so on. This great economic storm centre is moving into our economic weather pattern, and it is not being taken seriously enough. Another huge economic storm centre, one which has been using up world resources at an unprecedented rate, is that of the armaments race. Yet, interestingly enough, when we come into the House of Commons rarely do we hear about those two factors which have such a great influence on things taking place in this country, and which in part are responsible for the man in North Batt-leford, Saskatchewan or Windsor, Ontario, having to pay 20 per cent interest to buy a house. It is because of these two factors in the economic world, and the influence they are having, that one economist told me last week, a man whom I greatly appreciate for his understanding, that he does not know what is happening. He does not know where we are going. That is a problem the world community must face. I think what is important is that we look seriously at these factors as something which will change the traditional way in which our economies have worked.
Now, Mr. Speaker, on the question of linkage between countries around the world, I would say we are in a situation not unlike the situation which took place in the Montreal forum ten years ago when the Russian national hockey team came to Canada to play the Canadian national hockey team. Canadians knew that Canada could beat the U.S.S.R. We would just go down and laugh at them as they lost. If anyone remembers the first game and the kind of feeling we had inside after the game ended, you knew that the simplistic idea that Canada was the best hockey country in the world was over. Now we can go back and make up new theories about why it happened, but the fact was that Canada's national hockey team had been beaten in Canada by another country's national hockey team. 1 can remember the shock that was felt by every Canadian that week as we struggled through that very interesting hockey series. What is happening now in our economic world in Canada is not unlike what we lived in, in the hockey world, prior to that game.
I do not believe, for instance, that the automobile industry in North America, which was so solidly implanted here, will ever be quite the same as it was before the Japanese became the world's automobile maker. The auto industry may blossom again here, but it will never really be the same. There has been an economic hurricane, Mr. Speaker, which has changed forever our way of looking at the economic picture. In the
Supplementary Borrowing Authority
report of the parliamentary task force on North-South relations, on which I worked a few years ago, there is a recommendation contained in the last section under trade which is extremely important for Canada today. We recommended that the Government launch immediately a major public inquiry into the industrial sectors which are likely to be at a long-term competitive disadvantage in relationship to developing countries, with a view to developing effective adjustment measures. These adjustment measures are hard to accept because it means that the old way is over and a new way has begun.
The other economic storm, the armaments race, costs $600 billion a year. We are talking about $4 billion here tonight, and that is an impossible number to imagine, but $600 billion is what the world is spending on arms today. The two major powers are, in a sense, causing their economies to break down because of this race. The armaments race itself will lead to nothing except the destruction of the world. As we face the reality of the economics of the family down the street, of friends or neighbours, I think it is important that we understand where a great part of the problem comes from. I am going to make a few points about the amount of money that is taken out of the common pool and put into this area. I am no economist, that is obvious to everybody, but I know a few rules about what makes some things work. I think one market rule is that if you are short of a commodity, the price goes up, so if you are short of money, the interest goes up; it costs more to get money when there is not a lot available, and it costs less when there is money available.
One of the areas where money is being sucked up, we might say, at an incredible rate without any responsibility for what is happening to it, is in the arms race. The Pentagon is the centre of the arms race on this side of the world, but the same would be true on the other side of the world. The War Department, the patron of nuclear war, is the most powerful institution in history. As I understand it, there has never been an institution with as much physical power as the Pentagon. It has been estimated that the Pentagon has $1.5 trillion in assets. That is more than the total of all corporation stocks on the New York Stock Exchange. That is a shocking statistic, Mr. Speaker. It has 3,970 installations, an average of 80 for every State in the Union; it owns 25,000,000 acres of land; controls 400 major bases and 300 lesser bases in nearly every country in the world; it has 350 bases bordering the U.S.S.R.; it has 1.5 million military personnel in 116 nations; it is the largest consumer of capital and technology in the world; more than 60 per cent of all research and development funds in the United States go to the Pentagon or to the military; and more than one-third of the engineering personnel and scientists graduating from the universities go to the military.
These funds, taken from the economies of the world today, flow right into the life of every person. This affects me, it affects you, Mr. Speaker, and it affects everyone else because it makes money hard to get. At the same time, it deprives us of development funds that could be used for the good of the world.
